With a strong sensor, decent specs, and a smart hot-swappable battery system, I like pretty much everything about the MC7 other than the mouse itself, which is ugly, unwieldy, and not as comfortable as I'd like.

PC Gamer's got your back Our experienced team dedicates many hours to every review, to really get to the heart of what matters most to you. Find out more about how we evaluate games and hardware.

I must admit, I was mighty intrigued by the idea of a modern mouse (and all their high DPI machinations) with a screen slapped on the side, but I must also admit I thought we would be over the growing pains by now, what with screens being slammed into everything from cases to coolers to controllers.

Yet one look at the Turtle Beach Command Series MC7 suggests those growing pains are still being suffered. And using the mouse only confirms it.

But I get the idea in concept. I'm a big fan of my Stream Deck, and find myself regularly using its many controls. Being able to shove those into the side of the mouse with clarity to read what they're doing is intriguing. It's also particularly effective when it comes to swapping DPI, polling rate, and even checking the battery. Those are things that do benefit from a visual component. And yet a few weeks with the MC7 have convinced me I won't be making the swap full time.

✅ You gotta have a large screen on your mouse: As far as I can see, this is the only gaming mouse with modern specs and a big screen from a reputable brand out there.

❌ You want a mouse for competitive gaming: The MC7 is simply not comfortable nor snappy enough for competitive gaming❌ You don't need a large screen on your mouse: We've seen small OLED screens from the likes of SteelSeries and CoolerMaster if you're simply looking for something to display figures.

With a strong sensor, decent specs, and a smart hot-swappable battery system, I like pretty much everything about the MC7 other than the mouse itself, which is ugly, unwieldy, and not as comfortable as I'd like.

Wired and wireless (2.4 GHz and Bluetooth)

Internally, the MC7 has impressive stats. Its Owl-Eye Optical sensor goes all the way up to a max DPI of 30,000, and the polling rate of 8,000 Hz is competitive-level. That's so high, in fact, that the average person won't even see the benefit of it.

And the elephant in the room here: the 2.25-inch colour display is touch-sensitive too, which means you can flick through a couple of different screens depending on your use case. We have seen screens on gaming mice before, like the Cooler Master MM830 and SteelSeries Rival 710 (neither of which are touch screens), but as far as I can tell, the MC7 is the largest on a modern gaming mouse from a reputable brand. That makes it an oddity at the least.

But that's not all the MC7 has going for it. The 4D scroll wheel means you can go up, down, left and right on a page with just the wheel, and you have extra buttons here, too. You have one at the bottom of the thumb rest, another next to the mouse wheel, plus two on the left-hand side, as well as your standard clicks.

It's a wireless mouse, so it comes with a 2.4 GHz receiver, and it also has hot-swappable batteries. The battery charger has a spare USB Type-A port, which means your charger can also be the receiver. This is a sweet system, which makes the MC7 feel like it has infinite battery (as long as you are willing to spend twenty seconds swapping the battery every 10 or so hours).

The PC Gamer Circuit Breaker newsletter breaks down the latest PC gaming tech, and finds you the best deals on the best products

The Owl-Eye sensor is great. It's consistent and smooth, and never posed any problems in any of the games I threw this mouse at. For everyday gaming, I don't have any complaints about how its internals performed. It's a slightly customised version of the PixArt PAW3950 sensor, and will be familiar to anyone who's used the Razer Deathadder V3 Pro, which previously had the exclusive use of PixArt's 30K sensor.

The mouse clicks are a tad loud for my liking, but they're plenty snappy. This bad boy is fitted with Titan Optical switches, and they are perfect under my fingertips. I have yet to hit a single double-click and find them to be very responsive.

However, the biggest problem with performance is how the MC7's weight is balanced and how it feels under the palms. At 135 g grams, it's a fairly heavy mouse (more so than the recent Naga V3 Pro and its mountain of buttons), but this wouldn't be too big of a problem if it could balance that weight in a comfortable way.

However, it feels clunky, and even has a slight rattle at high speeds. This all contributes to a mouse that feels a little lacking in competitive play, even though it's got the internal chops to handle everything on paper.

In use, the screen is rather peculiar. Via the Turtle Beach Swarm II software, you can flit between a few screens, which you customise with your own controls, and they are fairly snappy and responsive. However, having to arch my fingers to actually click on the screen means it's not intended for quick play. That makes it better as a micro function, or a way of displaying battery (but the device's lighting can already indicate battery life and DPI setting). It can display things like health and ammo in Counter-Strike 2, but its viewing angles are pretty poor, meaning it doesn't offer much of a tactical advantage.

The MC7 comes with two 1000 mAh batteries, both of which are hot-swappable. They connect to a charger (which also has a USB port for your 2.4 GHz connector), and this means you technically only need one USB to do everything for your mouse. It's a great system.

To swap the batteries out, you simply take off a compartment where your palm rests, pull the battery out and put a new one in. The MC7's onboard battery is just big enough that I've never noticed the device dying while I'm changing batteries. It's pretty sweet, and with a little practice, it can be swapped in seconds. It's not quite as quick to swap as the Glorious Model O Eternal, with its open battery system, but it is a bit tidier.

Working on my PC every day, then gaming most nights, I found myself swapping out the battery every few days at 1,000 Hz polling, which is perfectly solid given how convenient swapping the batteries is.

The MC7 is a very confusing mouse in regard to its ergonomics. The groove on the left-hand side for your thumb is comfortable and intuitive, yet the two buttons on either side of that groove are awkward to get to. My left thumb buttons on a mouse tend to be going forward and backwards on a page, and therefore I like to have instant access to them. I don't have that access here, and have to physically bend my thumb or extend it to get to each button. The groove also has a texture to it, which is clearly designed so the mouse doesn't slip, and that's also quite strange, as it feels like you aren't encouraged to move your thumb, and yet you have to in order to hit those two buttons.

The back of the mouse curves to my palm well, but the two mouse click buttons are quite curved in the centre. That means, if I hold my hand on the bottom of the mouse, there's air underneath the bottom of my fingers as I hold it, and if I put my palm forward, then there's air underneath my knuckles. I feel like, no matter what way I hold the mouse, I'm holding it just a little wrong.

That's before getting to the screen, a panel that is too long to use all of it while on the go, and close enough to my fingers that I constantly change my DPI whenever I take my hand off the mouse and put it back on again. Perhaps the strangest element of this is that I couldn't seem to figure out a way to lock the screen, which would really make it much better for gaming.

For quickly changing a song or pausing a video, I actually found myself taking my left finger off the left click and wrapping it around the display instead. As far as I can tell, there just isn't a quick and comfortable way to get to all parts of the screen with ease, and I have quite large hands too.

As far as build quality is concerned, the MC7 doesn't feel cheap under the palm, though I'm not a fan of the vibration you get when you click the screen. It just has a hollow feel and sound. The texture on the mouse is cool to the fingertips, and it handles fingerprints well. Despite the fact that you have to take the back cover off to pop the batteries in, I could never get it to come off accidentally either, which is always a plus.

There is a slight rattle if you pick up the mouse and shake it, and that rattle appears to be coming from the 4D mouse wheel. Generally, you don't tend to shake mice, but if you pick it up quickly to move it from one side of the mousepad to the other, it does produce the rattling sound.

One thing I do quite like is a button sunken into the left thumbgrip. I can hold that down and move the rather great-feeling scroll wheel to change volume in an instant, and this is handier and quicker than using the touch screen's volume icons.

The MC7 is clearly intended to fit in alongside the likes of the Turtle Beach Stealth Pro II with its combination of copper and black, but it doesn't have the sleekness of its headset counterpart. Instead, it's more Cronenbergian, a collection of skewed angles and bumps, like the tech parts inside its shell are clamouring to get out and your hand is the thing holding them in. It's almost like two separate gaming mice have accidentally stepped inside the teleporter and what has come out is a wretched combination of both.

The right-hand side is relatively low to the ground and with little detailing, whereas the left side is angular, sharp and tall. This is naturally so tall because there's a screen slapped on the side, but it means the entire mouse has a slant going to the right.

Despite this slant, the front is cut at quite a sharp angle too. The MC7 is kind of curvy, and kind of not. It's kind of angular, and also kind of not. It's a hard shape to make sense of and, to my eyes, pretty darn ugly on top of my desk.

One element I do like about the MC7's aesthetic is its choice of RGB. You get a sleek line of it just underneath the mouse, which is customizable, but it glows red when the battery is low, which is a good reminder when I've needed it. The screen also alerts you when your battery is low.

As far as the display is concerned, it has colour, which is a nice touch, but also has weirdly poor viewing angles. If I look at the screen from the position I'd usually game from, it can look washed out. It never looks so washed out that I can't roughly guess what its icons are (and with time, you learn their position anyway), but it makes it feel less quality than the black and copper might suggest.

For the first few weeks with this mouse, I found Turtle Beach's Swarm II to be a mostly fine bit of software, though it could be a little slow. However, this week, the latest update, Software version 1.0.0.63 (which launched on November 2), has seemingly entirely broken on my PC. I can't get it to open, though it remains open in Task Manager. Given it only just launched, I could see this issue being fixed quickly, but it's a shame that so much software for hardware is not consistent.

It is also a necessary bit of software if you would like to customise the screen. With it downloaded, the screen is customizable much like a Stream Deck. Grab widgets from within the app, the mouse's onboard memory, or third-party apps, slap them on the screen, and now you have a new shortcut. Without it, there's not much you can do.

And, as far as I can tell, you can't set totally custom controls, as you can do with the Stream Deck, which limits your customisation a tad. But it's still pretty broad for the most part, and I've rarely found myself looking for a shortcut and not been able to find it.

$160 is a lot of cash for a gaming mouse. It's so much money, in fact, that you can pick up the best gaming mouse out there, the Razer Viper V4 Pro, with its impeccable sensor, great battery life, and lightweight feel, for the same price.

As such, you can pick an overall better, lighter mouse for the same price, or go for the screen. The battery system is certainly neat, though there are other mice out there with hot-swappable batteries.

The MC7 doesn't detract from day-to-day gaming, but I'd much prefer a lower base polling rate if it meant a cheaper price point, as this isn't exactly a competitive-level mouse in function.

It is clear where the budget for this build goes. A large screen couldn't be cheap; the material feels good on the fingertips, and that's before mentioning the research and development costs associated with getting a touchscreen on a mouse. However, it's so much money that, to my palms, it only really feels like the first step for Turtle Beach. It's like a test run of what a touchscreen could be like, and for this price, I don't quite see the vision.

3. Best budget wireless: Mchose G3 V2 Pro

4. Best budget wired: Glorious Model O Eternal

5. Best competitive:Logitech G Pro X2 Superstrike

6. Best lightweight: Corsair Sabre V2 Pro

7. Best MMO: Corsair Scimitar Elite Wireless SE

With a strong sensor, decent specs, and a smart hot-swappable battery system, I like pretty much everything about the MC7 other than the mouse itself, which is ugly, unwieldy, and not as comfortable as I'd like.

In that time, he has covered the latest doodads, contraptions, and gismos, and loved every second of it. Hey, it’s better than writing case briefs.

EAEaster EggStar WarsStar Wars Jedi: Survivor

Star Wars Jedi: Survivor was released back in 2023 and is a very good game with some fun Easter eggs and references hidden in it. But one secret remained hidden, even after the developer who included it in the third-person action game teased fans online about it. Now, someone has finally found the secret after inputting the Konami code in a menu.

Back in 2025, Respawn UI director Jordan DeVries posted cryptically on social media about a secret buried in Jedi: Survivor that players had yet to find. “Imagine shipping a (submitted, approved) UI easter egg in your game that no one has yet noticed or found,” posted the developer last year. That kicked off some players digging around the Soulslike Star Wars sequel for this hidden secret. But nobody seemingly found it until now, according to DeVries.

On November 1, DeVries shared on social media that user TowerBunga on Twitter had found the Easter egg after inputting the famous Konami code in the Force upgrade menu in Jedi: Survivor. And once entered correctly, a giant space frog appears and eats a strange moon in the sky. It’s a bizarre but amusing secret that took three years to find.

#3772. Activision to remove Itaewon crowd crush footage from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 and apologises to victims' families

"We bow our heads in deep sympathy and apology to the bereaved families and victims."

Activision has apologised to the bereaved families of the Itaewon crowd crush victims and confirmed it will remove real footage of the tragedy from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

In a new statement reported by Inven Global, Activision said the footage "will be completely removed" via a game update scheduled to roll out on 12th November.

The statement was issued in Korean, and the quotes come via Inven Global's AI-assisted, editor-reviewed translation.

As we reported earlier this week, the game's opening cinematic uses short news clips to depict fictional civilian casualties during a North Korean invasion of South Korea. Those clips have since been found to include archive footage from the 2022 Itaewon disaster, in which around 160 people died. The bereaved families' association and the Citizens Countermeasure Meeting called for its removal.

"We bow our heads in deep sympathy and apology to the bereaved families and victims who were deeply hurt by this incident, as well as to everyone we have caused concern," Activision said.

The publisher also said that Modern Warfare 4 "is a work of fiction created to provide realistic immersion", and it "never intended to evoke or trivialise any tragic event, including the Itaewon crowd crush" by using real news broadcast footage.

The controversy has also reached the South Korean government. During a press briefing, minister of the interior and safety Yun Ho-jung described the footage's inclusion as "secondary harm", and said: "I believe appropriate sanctions should be imposed".

"Using such a tragedy as material for a game, a form of entertainment or business, is something that should be refrained from as a matter of human ethics," Yun added. He said it was up to the relevant agencies to decide "whether to impose punishment or block it to make general access difficult".

Activision's earlier statement to Eurogamer said the opening cinematic "utilises some real world news coverage to establish the game's fictional narrative", and was "not intended to reference or trivialise the Itaewon disaster or any other real-world tragedy in any way, shape or form".

Rosario Dawson and Hayden Christensen know exactly how to get Star Wars fans worked up. Put them together, add a little Anakin-and-Ahsoka nostalgia, and people are already paying attention. Wrap both actors in sheer blue fabric so they look suspiciously like Force ghosts, and suddenly everyone starts wondering whether Dave Filoni is trying to tell us something about an upcoming movie release or another new Star Wars project. That is exactly what happened after Dawson shared a photo with Christensen that put a very funny spin on their Ahsoka connection.

In an Instagram post, the two Star Wars mainstays are not actually dressed as Ahsoka Tano and Anakin Skywalker. Christensen appears to be wearing regular clothes under a layer of translucent blue layer, while Dawson wears what looks more like a medieval or fantasy costume. If anything, the dress gives off a little Princess Fiona energy. See for yourself in her post below:

A post shared by rosariodawson (@rosariodawson)

Dawson made the joke even more obvious with her caption: “MAY THE FORCE GHOSTS BE WITH YOU 👻👻.”

The costumes are goofy, simple and immediately recognizable. Christensen looking like a Force ghost is also perfectly reasonable within Star Wars movie canon. Dawson getting the same treatment, however, is where fans started getting nervous. Because, uh… Why is Rosario Dawson a Force ghost?

To be clear, nobody at Lucasfilm announced the death of Ahsoka Tano's death through an Instagram costume photo. Dawson is not dressed as Ahsoka here, and there is no reason to think she casually spoiled one of the biggest possible developments in Ahsoka Season 2. That didn't stop fans from noticing the implication and asking a ton of questions.

Comments under the Clerks 2 actress's post quickly filled with people who remembered that becoming a Force ghost usually requires a fairly serious prerequisite. Fans wrote:

I understand the reaction. Ahsoka has survived Order 66, Darth Vader, the World Between Worlds and enough lightsaber fights to make most Jedi reconsider the profession entirely. She has also spent years bouncing between animated and live-action Star Wars, becoming one of the franchise's most durable characters in the process.

Christensen as a Jedi specter has precedent. Anakin appeared as a Force ghost at the end of Ahsoka Season 1, and the original trilogy was later reworked to insert the actor into the old footage. Christensen is also returning for Season 2, with Anakin expected to remain part of Tano's story.

Dawson's Ahsoka, meanwhile, is still very much alive when Season 2 begins. She and Sabine Wren remain stranded beyond the known galaxy while Grand Admiral Thrawn has returned home and prepares for whatever comes next. So when the actress playing her suddenly appears next to Anakin's actor, both covered in ghostly blue fabric, fans will read into it.

For now, though, I am choosing the much less stressful explanation. They found some blue fabric, put it over their heads, and somebody took a photo. Nobody is dying. Probably.

Season 2 of Ahsoka hits the streaming calendar on January 20, 2027, for everyone with a Disney+ subscription. Fans can also stream all of the Star Wars movies -- including the prequels featuring Hayden Christensen -- using that same membership.

#3770. PUBG live-action series in the works at Netflix, with Donald Glover set to direct and star

PUBG is being turned into a live-action series for Netflix, with Donald Glover set to direct, write, executive produce, and star.

Krafton announced the adaptation on 30th October, adding that Glover's brother Stephen, his writing partner on Atlanta, will join the project as a writer and executive producer.

The series will also be executive produced by Michael Schaefer for Neon TV, Fam Udeorji for Gilga, and Taeseok Jang and Sujin Lee for LV3H. LV3H is Krafton's entertainment arm, and it's involved in both developing and producing the show.

There's no word yet on a release window, plot, or who else will star.

Glover is a two-time Emmy and Golden Globe winner, best known for Atlanta and Community. Krafton calls PUBG "one of the world’s most enduring gaming franchises", and says the game, which is credited with popularising the battle royale genre, holds seven Guinness World Records.

Earlier this month, Krafton revealed it was ending development of PUBG: Black Budget, the extraction shooter spin-off announced nearly a year ago. The publisher’s other games include Subnautica and InZoi.

#3769. Call of Duty: Warzone’s yearly refresh includes DMZ map Hajin in BR, MW4 guns, and reworks galore

Call of Duty’s Warzone is once again getting refreshed, this time to coincide with season one of Modern Warfare 4 this week.

Starting on Nov. 6, the new Hajin map from DMZ and MW4’s campaign will make its way to Warzone as a new battle royale experience, becoming the seventh different large-scale map to play home to the last-player-standing mode since the game launched in 2020.

The same locations found within Hajin in DMZ are on display here, bringing forth a new Gulag location and even the Korean-themed locale’s dynamic weather. The map will also include MW4’s weapons and mechanics, such as the ability to drag downed allies, and the new game’s weapons will now be the main loot pool for BR and Resurgence. Needless to say, those who’ve been playing MW4 since launch will be at an advantage out of the gate when it comes to crafting loadouts.

All weapons from Modern Warfare 2 (2022) through Black Ops 7 (2025) will be usable in Warzone, but they cannot be edited in the Gunsmith, so they are basically defunct. But many cosmetics like operators, operator skins, finishing moves, emblems, etc. will still be available in Warzone for season one of MW4.

New MW4 gameplay features in Warzone include a Zipline Launcher field upgrade to reach new heights, a rebalancing of Perks to equip into your loadouts, and a slew of new equipment like all of MW4’s killstreaks and more. And this is all in addition to new content coming for MW4 multiplayer and DMZ as well.

As for the respawn-enabled Resurgence, the new map Zodiac will also become the main attraction after appearing earlier this year as part of MW4’s beta. Nagoshi Studio revealed Gang of Dragon less than a year ago, but it ran into trouble just a few months later.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Six months after the disappearance of Nagoshi Studio's website, a Google-translated notice in the Japan government's Kanpo website (via Gematsu) says the company has now officially closed its doors.

Founded by Yakuza creator Toshihiro Nagoshi in 2021 after a run of more than 30 years at Sega, Nagoshi Studio's first game was revealed at the 2025 Game Awards as Gang of Dragon—although the reveal was really just a brief CGI clip of Ma Dong-Seok that could have been lifted straight from Korean action film The Outlaws.

The wheels came off just a few months later, though, when NetEase pulled funding for the studio, amidst a broader pullback from external studio support over the previous year. Nagoshi Studio reportedly had no success finding another benefactor to fill the gap, and two months later, in May, the studio's website disappeared.

No official proclamations about the fate of the studio were forthcoming, though, and the Steam page remained online, so faint hope of a last-minute rescue persisted. Now, I'm afraid even that's gone, although the Steam listing is still up if you want to poke around at what might have been.

#3767. Pikmin 4 Nintendo Switch 2 Edition launches 12th November and a demo is out tomorrow

Pikmin 4 Nintendo Switch 2 Edition will launch on 12th November, bundled with a new mode called Dandori Academy.

Nintendo confirmed the date during yesterday's surprise Pikmin Day Direct, which also revealed that a demo will land on the Nintendo eShop on 2nd November. Any progress you make in the demo will transfer to the full game if you buy it.

Dandori Academy is a timed exam mode. The Direct showed off one of its exams, Gargantuan Garden, which challenges players to collect gold nuggets before time runs out (thanks, Insider Gaming).

The Switch 2 Edition will also let you give voice commands to Oatchi, the game’s dog companion. If you already own Pikmin 4 on the original Switch, you can buy an upgrade pack from the eShop.

Nintendo had warned ahead of the broadcast that there would be no new game announcements. Instead, Shigeru Miyamoto introduced Japanese actor Fuka Koshiba as a new ambassador for the series, and Nintendo confirmed that 1st November, today, is now Pikmin Day.

Pikmin 4 originally launched on Switch in July 2023. The Switch 2 Edition is one of two big Nintendo releases this month, alongside The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake on 5th November.

Legendary Nintendo developer Shigeru Miyamoto - who directed classic games such as Super Mario 64 and produced The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time - recently argued that the rise of generative AI tools won't necessarily replace human talent.

90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way's Andi Wallace and Nigel have me going back and forth on whether they'll stick together amidst issues navigating ethical non-monogamy. There were obvious red flags suggesting this couple wouldn't last until the end of the season. However, thanks to some recent updates, I'm not so sure now.

When I first learned about Andi being on Tinder, I assumed this was an open-and-shut case. Gone were the days of roaming supermarkets without shoes on. Now, I'm not sure what to think, and I'm eager to see the rest of this storyline play out on the 2026 TV schedule due to two new developments cropping up.

Halloween just came and went, and Andi had a pretty interesting choice for her costume. She went as Nigel, and mimicked a viral photo of him that's made rounds on the internet as of late. Take a look:

A post shared by Andi Jane (@andijanemusic)

Generally speaking, I don't think many people are in the habit of dressing up as their exes for Halloween. I've seen couples go as each other, or even as other couples. Is Andi dressing up like this because she wants to appease the 90 Day Fiancé fans, or is she paying tribute to her current fiancé? I'm not quite sure, because I'd wager most watching on TLC or with an HBO Max subscription wouldn't get this reference. However, that's just speculation on my part.

While Andi is dressing up like Nigel, the man himself is traveling across the world and hanging out with Azrael, the blue-haired woman recently introduced on 90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way. Reddit has photos of them together chopping it up, dancing and kissing at some sort of music festival.

90 Day Fiancé's Shea Looks Almost Unrecognizable To Me After Weight Loss

Based on Andi's statements on feeling uncomfortable about Nigel and Azrael's relationship, I can't imagine she'd approve of that. In fact, she's been a bit alarmed by how many partners Nigel's had amid their time apart and has kept pushing for a monogamous relationship now that she's in Australia.

Given these recent developments, I can't tell if this means Andi has embraced the polyamorous lifestyle or not. It could be possible they're still together and that by the end of this season, she'll reveal she's made peace with him dating who he wants while she's away.

It's also possible Andi has simply decided this lifestyle isn't for her and harbors no ill feelings toward Nigel. He was, after all, pretty straight up about being polyamorous and said that asking him to stop that lifestyle was a deal-breaker. There's nothing wrong with Andi trying out a relationship to see if she can handle it, and ultimately realizing she wants someone who is exclusive to her.

Given all the uncertainty, I'm more eager than ever to see the latest episode of 90 Day Fiancé: The Other Way, which airs on TLC on Sundays at 8:00 p.m. ET. #3765. Dune: Awakening's free Blood and Ice expansion swaps sand for snow on 1st December

Funcom's survival MMO Dune: Awakening is heading north with a free expansion that trades the deserts of Arrakis for a frozen new map.

The expansion, called Blood and Ice, will release on 1st December. Funcom said it adds "around 35 hours of new progression", along with new vehicle modules, augments, and specialisation traits. It's coming to PC, PS5, and Xbox.

The new map, called the Polar Sink, turns the game's usual survival loop upside down. Instead of protecting yourself from extreme heat, you'll need to find ways to stay warm, upgrading your gear with resources found only in the Polar Sink.

The map is split into two biomes, the tundra and the ice cap. You'll start in the tundra, where wealthy water shipper families have built lavish strongholds, before trying to get into the heavily guarded ice cap. Once you're in, you can harvest ice to cool your base equipment and speed up production.

According to Funcom, the expansion "brings the focus back to ground-level survival, with traversal, temperature management, and combat all playing important roles in your progression". The studio also said future updates will add more reasons to go back to the region.

Blood and Ice also brings a new Events tab to the main menu. Shortly after the expansion launches, a new event called Water Crisis will follow the current one, The Scourge. Funcom says every event can be completed in both single-player and multiplayer, and that it plans to run them more often, each with new stories and free rewards.

Funcom has also launched a cosmetics store, which it says will help fund continued development and free updates. The store will start with a rotating selection of items, including looks taken from the Dune films to coincide with Dune: Part Three's release in cinemas this December. The plan is to eventually make the full catalogue available at all times.

Several of the community's most-requested features are also on the way. Offline single-player is due this month, and from January 2027 you'll be able to copy characters from multiplayer servers to single-player, and from single-player to select private or self-hosted servers on PC. Full cross-play will also arrive in January 2027.

"We're far from done," Funcom said, adding that it has "ambitious plans for the year ahead", including major free updates in 2027. The studio says more than a million new players have joined since the game launched on consoles, alongside a rebuilt endgame, three DLCs, and the conclusion of the game's first story arc, Book One.

Just a couple of weeks ago, Norwegian developer Funcom, creator of Dune: Awakening and Conan Exiles - and many other games - confirmed it was entering a period of restructuring and bracing for layoffs as a result. You may remember the company making a similar move this time last year, months after the initial PC release of Dune: Awakening.

#3764. A 21-Year Veteran Of Xbox Who Is Suddenly No Longer At The Company Says She Has ‘Serious Concerns’ About The Whole Process

Helen Chiang had been at Microsoft since 2005. She spent over a decade overseeing Minecraft, the company’s most important gaming franchise, and survived this year’s big Xbox “reset” with a promotion to the role of the gaming division’s chief operating officer. Barely three months later, she’s suddenly out at the company she called home for more than two decades, a development which generated tons of speculation about whether she was fired or not. Chiang now says she’s breaking her silence to set the record straight.

“There has been some speculation about my abrupt departure from Microsoft, including claims that I was ‘fired for a policy violation,'” she wrote on LinkedIn, referencing a report last month from Eurogamer alleging she was fired for a “policy violation.” “Thatâs not accurate and while I wonât turn this into a play-by-play, silence should not be mistaken for agreement. What has been said about my departure, and what has been left unsaid, has created a picture of me that I hardly recognize. Itâs important to me to set the record straight.”

Chiang went on to say that she never leaked confidential company information to the press or went outside of company-authorized communication channels. She said she also did not leave the company for a competitor, nor did she “engage in discrimination, bullying, harassment, insider trading, embezzlement, or other fraudulent activity.” Chiang added that her past results and record speak for themselves, and that she did not leave the company because she’d been passed over for a bigger role. The chief operating officer role had not been something she’d lobbied for.

“I believe in fairness, accountability, and holding ourselves to the standards we expect of others,” she wrote. “Those standards only mean something when theyâre applied consistently. I have serious concerns about how they were applied in my case, and I believe those concerns deserve to be taken seriously. I share this because I donât want my departure reduced to an inaccurate story about incompetence, ambition for the next big job, or a Nelson-level scandal. My story is about staying true to your core values, especially when it is hard. Thatâs the legacy I hope to leave behind.”

“We donât discuss individual personnel matters,” a spokesperson for Microsoft previously told Kotaku regarding Chiang’s departure. “Weâre grateful for Helen’s years of service and wish her well.”

The sudden move comes amid a massive reorganization of Xbox that has seen massive layoffs and studio divestitures as Microsoft seeks to rebuild the platform while also improving its bottom line. As chief operating officer, Chiang would have had a central role in helping to restructure and better optimize the tech giant’s gaming business ahead of the next console generation, Project Helix, which is reportedly set to arrive in 2028. Though the Xbox veteran set out to clear the air amid much of the recent speculation about her departure from the company, it’s still not clear what exactly happened.

“For the first time, we are establishing a Chief Operating Officer with end-to-end P&L responsibility across content, hardware, platform, and services,” Xbox CEO Asha Sharma wrote back in July. “Helen Chiang has been promoted to this role and will report directly to me. Over nearly two decades at XBOX, Helen has helped build some of our most important businesses, from XBOX Live to leading Mojang and the Minecraft franchise. She will bring our businesses together under one operating model, making sure we make clear investment decisions, learn from our successes and failures, and hold ourselves accountable for results.”

Sharma later told The Wall Street Journal “clarity is kindness” when describing the tough choices she was making to set the stage for an ambitious future. “Clarity is Kindness” is also how Chiang began her LinkedIn post today. âThis is not how I ever imagined my story here would end,” she wrote. “And it is not the whole story.â

#3761. Footage of a Persona 1 remake has seemingly leaked online

Almost two minutes of footage from what appears to be a remake of the original Persona has leaked online.

The clip, which seemingly gives the remake the subtitle Be Your True Mind, was shared on the GamingLeaksAndRumours subreddit. It was uploaded to file-sharing site Gofile on 31st October under a Japanese filename that translates as "Megami Ibunroku Persona Remake".

Interestingly, the footage looks a lot like Atlus' more recent entries. It shows off stylish menus and a brief look at combat that closely resembles Persona 5 and Persona 3 Reload. There's also a short social link cutscene in a noticeably different, almost graphic novel art style.

Fans digging through the clip believe they have spotted several details that lend it credibility. These include what looks like Unreal Engine debug text in the top left corner during battle (Atlus switched to Unreal Engine for Persona 3 Reload), a new remix of the original PlayStation game's Pandora theme, and the protagonist being referred to as "Boy With Earring", which is how he is named in Persona 2: Eternal Punishment.

Atlus has not announced a Persona 1 remake, and we can't verify the footage, so treat all of this with the usual caveats.

How do you solve a problem like Persona 4? At Gamescom, we sat down with series director Kazuhisa Wada to talk about the Persona 4 Remake, and ask about how Atlus is approaching the original text for the remake.

I think this would be as big a hit as the books.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I'm buzzing through the Dungeon Crawler Carl series this year, and my 8-year-old daughter gets so jealous every time she sees it. She loves cats, dinosaurs, and adventure, so in her mind, there's no reason she shouldn't be able to read it as well or watch the upcoming series when it premieres for those with a Peacock subscription.

Of course, anyone who has read the books knows that they're hardly appropriate for a young audience. One would have to remove all the gore, swearing, and raunchy jokes for it to even begin to pass for most parents, which gave me an idea. What if Princess Donut was able to retell the events of DCC, but in the way she'd tell it to her dinosaur "child," Mongo?

I love the way Princess Donut treats and refers to Mongo like he's a child, despite the fact that he's a raptor regularly tearing their enemies to bits. She's always worried about him being traumatized, or "appalled," which got me thinking. It would be hilarious to read Donut recalling their past adventures to Mongo, and self-censoring the raunch along the way.

I just imagine my daughter laughing as I'd tell her about Princess Donut dancing in the club, zapping goblins with her laser vision, and going on side tangents about her hatred for Cocker Spaniels. It would still be the Donut we know from the books, but she's adjusting it all for the audience it's intended for.

I think it would be important to have that, rather than standard narration. Donut is a gem of a character, and I think introducing children to that early on would only encourage them to check out the novels in full when they're of age later in life.

I've often thought about Carl being the narrator in Dungeon Crawler Carl, and how much the story might change if it were anyone else narrating. The things they'd focus on, compared to him, and the things they'd notice well before he did. I'm of the opinion that Donut might have a more entertaining telling of it all, which is part of the reason she's just the best.

Matt Dinniman Can Thank Jeopardy! For Making Dungeon Crawler Carl's Success Feel Real For His Mom's Friends

All this to say, part of this plight is because I also want to see how much I'd enjoy Donut retelling the story, even if it were geared toward children. Plus, there are already spinoffs in the works, like the upcoming comic featuring Florin.

If I could get the ball rolling on making Princess Donut's Bedtime Stories For Mongo, I definitely would. I'm not the author, however, so Matt Dinniman, if you have time between making the rest of the series, perhaps consider this pitch to sell the fun of Dungeon Crawler Carl to the children?

In the meantime, I'll keep reading the stories, waiting for the new books and announcements related to the upcoming series. I have a feeling we're about to be overwhelmed with news about the franchise over the next year, but I promise I won't let it break me.

#3758. Modern Warfare 4 on Switch 2 has much worse input lag than PS5

Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 on Switch 2 has noticeably worse input lag than on PS5, which could put Nintendo players at a disadvantage in multiplayer.

Digital Foundry's tech review measured multiplayer latency at 81ms when docked and an average of 100ms in portable mode, against 49ms on PS5. Testing used wireless controllers on both consoles (a Switch 2 Pro Controller and a DualSense), and portable results ranged from 83ms at best to 125ms at worst.

Digital Foundry said "responsiveness here simply isn't as good as on other consoles", and described the lag in portable mode as "actually deleterious to performance" (thanks, IGN).

Beyond the lag, Digital Foundry is fairly positive about the port. Multiplayer runs at 60fps most of the time, and if your TV supports VRR, you'll notice the drops less. The campaign is capped at 30fps and resolution is dynamic.

Docked with DLSS on, the game targets 900p, but Digital Foundry saw it drop to 450p in busier scenes, such as the Paris vehicle chase. In portable mode, the target is 720p, with drops to 360p.

It's been 13 years since a Call of Duty game last appeared on Nintendo hardware, with Ghosts on Wii U in 2013. The series' return is the result of a 10-year deal Microsoft offered Nintendo while it sought regulatory approval for its $69 billion acquisition of Activision Blizzard.

Yesterday we reported that Activision has apologised to the bereaved families of the Itaewon crowd crush victims and confirmed it will remove real footage of the tragedy from Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4.

#3757. Developers, Creators, And Fans Remember BioWare: ‘I’ve Been Trying To Replicate That Feeling For Almost My Whole Life’

When I initially put out a call for fans, developers, creators, and media to reach out to me with stories about their experiences with BioWare, the now-shuttered developer of some of the most beloved western RPGs of the past 30 years, I was frankly overwhelmed by the outpouring of responses from people who had a story to tell. I was so overwhelmed, in fact, that I was only able to use a fraction of what showed up in my inbox for this collection of memories, praise, righteous anger, and mourning. Whether they were old heads who had been playing BioWare games since the days of Shattered Steel and the original Baldurâs Gate or folks who fell in love with the Edmonton studioâs work through Mass Effect and Dragon Age, itâs clear that BioWareâs games left an imprint on fans that has outlived the company itself.

(Submissions have been lightly edited for style and clarity.)

If BioWareâs games have proven anything, itâs that everyoneâs story has its own unique beginning, and thatâs reflected in how its fans came to know its work through so many different points of entry.

My first BioWare experience was with the first two Baldur’s Gate games. I wasn’t much of a PC CRPG gamer in 1998 but BG1 just absolutely blew me away with what, at the time, felt like endless options for character customization, the broad sweep of the story that felt like a true investment in the Dungeons & Dragons tabletop I had been playing for only a few years at that point – and the Forgotten Realms where I cut my teeth as both player and Dungeon Master – and the amazing writing on the characters. This doubled in effect when BG2 arrived in the year 2000, and between those two games I lived in BioWare’s Forgotten Realms like it was a second home. â Phil Morgan, host of Deleted Saves Podcast

I swiped Baldur’s Gate from my dad when I was nine – he wasn’t into role-playing games and I have no idea why he had it, but it clicked immediately for me and I spent hours trying different types of characters, killing NPCs I shouldn’t have, and getting to know that world. It blew me away when I realized I could recruit different party members in Baldur’s Gate, and that it had an impact on the story. It meant I could replay the game over and over and make different choices to see what would happen, and that became something BioWare was known for. â Chuck Zimmerheld, Giant Bomb

Years [after playing KOTOR], my next experience was attending a Video Games Live concert with conductor Jack Wall, who was the composer for the first two Mass Effect games, and that’s where I first heard the Mass Effect theme. That song was so beautiful to me that I knew I had to play the game it had come from. I didn’t have a lot of money at the time, but I scrimped and saved and got my brother to go half in with me on an Xbox 360. I bought a used copy of Mass Effect before we’d even gotten the Xbox, I was so excited. It blew my mind AGAIN in so many ways. A shooter RPG. A unique space adventure not tied to the IPs I’d enjoyed all my life. I fell in love with all of the unique characters and the idea of a space-faring future where humans weren’t the dominant species felt so fresh and exciting. â Jeremy Greco, BioWare fan

My first experience with BioWare, and one of my earliest memories of gaming in general, was watching my older brother play Dragon Age: Origins in 2010 on our PS3. I was frankly terrified watching it as an 8 year old. To this day, seeing the Darkspawn still conjures up a deep-rooted childhood fear of the Blight sweeping across the land. I remember playing through the game a few years later, thinking I was braver, and being absolutely horrified by the Circle Mage origin. I mean the Harrowing was insane to me. I think it took me maybe a week of going back and forth to finally finish that prologue. That game absolutely set the bar for me of dark heroic fantasy and hugely influenced my taste in games and stories ever since. â Jerram Carr, junior narrative designerÂ

BioWareâs games were the origin story for many developersâ own careers. You can trace the influences and inspirations that shaped the work of many designers and writers back to the worlds the company created.

I think the most impactful game for me was Dragon Age: Origins. I was in college excited for a new Bioware game, but at the same time struggling with accepting myself as a gay man. I had the chance to flirt with Alistair as a man, and while he ultimately rejected me, he helped me feel seen; that it was okay to be gay. I remember crying on the floor, moved that a 3D character had given me so much grace to be myself. I remember wanting to make games so people could have moments like I did. Moments to accept ourselves and see ourselves reflected positively.

When I did get the chance to make queer people feel seen in Destiny it felt like I was helping pay back the gift the DA:O team had given me. I even talked about it in the Bungie weekly blog.Â  â Nigel Davis, senior producer at Entangled Publishing, formerly at Bungie

The creators at BioWare pushed the industry forward with player choice in games. Optional party members, loyalty quests, morality systems, and huge choices with multi-game impacts. RPG’s aren’t the same without them. â Chuck Zimmerheld, Giant Bomb

Few studios can say that they changed the way genres are made. BioWare can. Thereâs an entire generation of developers and narrative designers that work in the industry because they were inspired by the games BioWare made across a 30-year run that largely produced classic after classic after classic. The systems the folks at BioWare designed worked their ways into other games in ways that you could see and interact with. My buddies and I used to joke that BioWare invented the wheel because Mass Effectâs dialogue wheel felt like it was everywhere after the original game was released. â Will Borger, journalist and consultant

For me, it all traces back to those first two Baldur’s Gate games. There’s a direct line from those to my work today, including my writing on Pacific Drive, where I’ve tried to remember to highlight the everyday as well as the extraordinary, to add jokes as well as drama, to imagine how even the smallest details shape the most fantastical world. And to remember that, if you hide a little secret somewhere, players will always, always find it. I think BioWare understood that players weren’t taking the roles of adventurers, but players are adventurers, always on the hunt for the next clue, character or collectible, and they really enjoyed indulging them as much as they could. â Paul Dean, writer, Pacific Drive

My time in development is not spent creating digital worlds (currently), I design mechanics for expressing actions and desires in the space of a world full of character interactions and player agency. Game theory is a lived experience because I love games, I play them, and they shaped me. Dungeons & Dragons is in some ways closer to my style of product, but it is not what I think of when I am writing. I’m thinking of Liara T’soni, Captain Anderson, Canderous Ordo, Jolee Bindo, Hawke, Varric, Blackwall, Dorian, Solas. â SalubriousBrew, pen and paper RPG developer

I wasnât a fan of much as a kid. I didnât like Star Wars, or RPGs, or games that looked older than me. I didnât even play KOTOR on a half decent console: my first playthrough was on my dadâs iPad! So when I, dorky Nigerian kid, got this weird-looking rpg on a whim, I couldnât have imagined that, well over a decade later, itâd be one of the main reasons I aspire to one day do narrative design for a video game.

Itâs not like I grew up reading stories about millionaire game writers or anything, lol. Iâm not in it for the money. I just think that making something that means to someone else what KOTOR meant for meâthatâd be pretty damn cool. â Mo, BioWare fan

BioWare was the first studio to show me that a game can tell a worthwhile story, that a game can make you cry and make you laugh. These days, I’m making games about fart jokes, but there’s a throughline from Garrus talking about “popping the heatsink” and Kasumi inspecting Shepard’s underwear drawer to what I do now. Other studios left more of a mechanical impact on my game development sensibilities, but BioWare showed me that games could be more than the sum of their parts. â Mira Swor, engineer at Jackbox Games

BioWareâs approach to roleplaying, and the prowess with which the studio pulled it off, became things many RPGs would aspire to replicate in the years that followed, and the opportunity its games provided to explore the perspectives of different types of people was more far-reaching in its impact than even the studio might haveÂ  expected, particularly when it chose to highlight queer characters and stories.

As a trans lesbian growing up closeted in a very rural, very conservative, very religious household in Florida, my opportunities to engage with queerness were deeply limited. When I went off to college, I was free to do what I wanted for the first time. My first week on campus, I walked down to the campus GameStop and bought Mass Effect 1, Mass Effect 2, Dragon Age: Origins, and Dragon Age II all at once by trading in some old games. I didnât really do it because I knew they were queer games. I just liked scifi and fantasy.

I popped in ME1 first. I had heard a lot of people praise Jennifer Haleâs performance as FemShep. That was enough of an excuse to bypass my repression, letting me create a female avatar for the first time ever. That alone was a really big deal for me, but the real paradigm shift happened the first time I realized I could flirt with Liara. I remember pausing at the choice for quite some time, feeling sick to my stomach with anxiety. Iâd been raised to believe that the feeling inside me that wanted to explore a lesbian romance was of the devil, a threat to my immortal soul. But ultimately, I forged ahead.

In a very real way, that was the first time I ever chose my burgeoning queerness. Iâd experienced queer feeling before, but always passively. This time I passed a threshold. â Saoirse Stone, BioWare fan, critic, author, Editor-In-Chief at Stone Freedom

Even just having queer characters and the ability to be queer in a mainstream AAA game without it being a joke resonated and reverberated so far through my life that it helped open my closet door just a little more. It was because of Mass Effect and Dragon Age that I got to explore sexuality and gender in a way that felt safe – in the comfort of my dorm room, sure, but also in the comfort of the worlds themselves. To see a gay relationship being celebrated or a trans person existing in the world as just a normal thing – it helped build my courage and eventually landed me where I am today: happy and comfortable in my body and in who I love. There aren’t many games that can say they helped people do that. â- Patrick Quinn, BioWare fan

My first experience with Bioware was Knights of the Old Republic. I grew up a big fan of the franchise and was really curious about a game that let me make all the decisions in it AND it let me play as a woman? I was sold from the jump. But upon exploring the game, seeing new worlds, getting to know my companions, I realized that even my queerness could be explored when I met Juhani at the Jedi Academy. It wasn’t a full romance, it didn’t even trigger real cutscenes. But the moment I learned I could get that conversation loop with her, I would visit her on the ship every time I could, hoping new dialog would loop in our Will They Won’t They. It was the first time I really felt seen as a baby butch in a game and it’s been a standard I’ve held games to ever since. â Erminia, Community Manager

I learned who I am through their games. Itâs not hyperbole. They helped me figure out the kind of person I would grow to be. As a pansexual nonbinary person their games were a safe space to experiment and experience things to see how it made me feel. The joy of falling for characters like Thane and Kaidan and knowing what that kind of love could feel like made me feel seen. Being able to play as a nonbinary Qunari in Dragon Age: The Veilguard and share my own gender journey with Taash to comfort them is one of the most gender-affirming experiences of my life. I never felt more confident about who I was than when I was playing one of their games. â Matt Storm aka Stormageddon, Podcast co-host for the âFunâ & Games Podcast and Reignite â A BioWare Replay Podcast

The passion people have for BioWare games is a shared one, and even though the company is gone, the communities its work fostered will persist long after publisher EA closes its doors. But itâs not just about having forums in which to talk about these games or places to post fan art or cosplay; several people had stories about how BioWareâs games established lifelong connections, made them feel closer to the ones already in their lives, or helped them see a path forward after a loss.

My dad was a submariner. He loves BioWare games, Mass Effect specifically. He saw me playing one day, and asked if I minded if he tried it out. He loves that series. I think he felt a connection to Shepard (specifically Jennifer Haleâs version) as a fellow ship captain. After he retired, the series became one of his projects. Heâs dedicated to the perfect playthrough. Heâs got what we call the Book of Knowledge. In it is the result of every dialogue choice, the location of every collectible (including the ones that arenât in the strategy guides), and how best to complete every quest. Itâs the most complete guide to those games I have ever seen. He has several characters running at once, records all of his playthroughs, and heâs turned that into a story heâs chronicling of his Shepard. Itâs not for anyone else; just him.

When I visit, we talk about Mass Effect and Dragon Age and he asks me when I think the next game is coming out. One year, for his birthday, the only thing he wanted was to hang out with me over the holidays and finish Mass Effect 3 because it was the one I hadnât finished, and he wanted to see how Iâd play it. Weâd sit there and compare choices, builds, talk about the characters. For several years, I just bought him models of the ships for birthdays and Christmas. Weâd go to cons and heâs trying to get the autographs of all the voice actors. It was something we could connect over even though we live on opposite ends of the country. I havenât spoken with him since the closure, partially because the thought of being the one to tell him breaks my heart. I know how much that series means to him, and how much respect he had for the folks who worked on every aspect of it.

I have a better relationship with my dad because of BioWareâs games. For me, thatâs their legacy. I hope the folks who worked there know how much the art they made meant to so many, and that their games connected us to the people we love. â Will Borger, journalist and consultant

While I was already a fan at the time, the most impactful moment for me – and one that solidified how deeply my love for BioWare would go – came in the midst of my grief over losing my mother to suicide in January 2012. Two months after her death, Mass Effect 3 was released. By that point, nothing was bringing me distraction or relief, not even my beloved video games, but I had already preordered it so I picked it up anyway. Played through the campaign, then decided to give BioWareâs first foray into multiplayer a try. It proved to be the only outlet at that time to take my mind off my pain and be elsewhere. Interacting with other fans in the community, fighting the Reapers together, and being head-butted between waves by a friendly Krogan was the catalyst for helping me feel a little bit like my old self again.

It gave me hope that I could find fun once more and could eventually reclaim my life from the depression Iâd fallen into. It was honestly the first time I had smiled and laughed since her death.

All that alone would have been impactful enough, but then things went deeper. BioWare was being lit up online about the Mass Effect 3 endings, and I felt bad for them after the game had personally helped me so much. I decided to write and mail off an old-fashioned letter to the Edmonton studio address, telling them my story and thanking them for creating a game that at least one fan really enjoyed and found succor in. I did it that way simply hoping it would actually be seen by the team rather than an email lost to the void somewhere in all the negative noise. The team not only received my letter, but passed it around and were incredibly touched by it.

So much so that I was surprised one day to find not only a letter back from them, but an autographed lithograph and other goodiesâ¦ including an âHonor The Fallenâ Normandy patch. Iâm tearing up again now 14 years later just remembering it. Chris Priestly, former BioWare community coordinator, wrote to me in that reply letter all those years ago: âWe often lose sight that our games can do more than be mere entertainment and, occasionally, can make a real difference.âÂ  â Tiffany Lowe, BioWare fan

Mass Effect 3 was particularly meaningful to me as it was released during a tumultuous time in my personal life. I was going through a divorce in which the mother of my child (only two at the time) had essentially vanished and left us alone. I was struggling not only with the loss, but with being a single parent all of a sudden. The few moments I got to play ME3 during that time were cathartic. Allowing me to focus on tasks I could handle. It kept me from wallowing. Truly, the “friends” I had in my companions helped pull me through the dregs of my depression and kept me from drowning.Â

All of their games have done something similar for me (I could go on and on), and if there’s anything I want the developers to know about their legacy, itâs this: their work mattered. Their stories touched my life in a way that not only set me on a path to telling my own stories as a professional writer (and writing about games), but got me through hard times. â Jordan Maison, BioWare fan and media

Veilguard came out at a weird time for me. My mother-in-law had died a couple years prior, two days after I had her first grandchild and a few hours after she got to hold that grandchild for the first and last time. We spent a year helping my husbandâs family adjust to this whole new life without the cornerstone of their family, and after that year we decided to sell the house to pay off my six-figure student loans. That plan worked out, but we spent the following year living together with my husbandâs family, mourning together and bringing new kids into a world without their grandmother. By the end of our year living there I had another newborn, lingering health issues from pregnancy, and a new house that I was being pushed to move into a week after giving birth. And then the 2024 election happened. I would not leave my room for weeks. I just wanted to hold my babies in bed where I felt safe.Â

I promised my husband that we could get a PS5 when we moved in, and one of the first games he bought was Veilguard specifically for me. I didnât really go in with expectations, and I hadnât replayed Inquisition in years, but it felt a lot like coming home. It made the family room feel as safe as the bedroom. I spent late nights running up and down the stairs to feed a baby every few hours between game chapters, but I really couldnât put it down.Â

I think it just helped to feel like the world wasnât falling apart, because in a game I have the power to fix it, and to give power to the people who feel powerless in the face of everything moving against them in the world. I was genuinely so engulfed in the story that I didnât realize Varric was dead. It hurt a lot to think that my guiding pillar in that space was gone. But it emphasized that I have the strength to do the things I was afraid to do without my mother-in-law and everyone else whoâs left us. (We actually had a slew of family deaths, but that was the most jarring.) I donât think Iâd be as well off mentally right now if I didnât have Veilguard at the right time. â Elam Bonebright, illustrator

At some point [while playing Dragon Age: Inquisition], I tweeted about how I needed to find someone else who had played it, anyone, because I was obsessed, and I had absolutely no idea how vast and passionate a fandom I had just alerted to my presence. What followed was 6 years of community and friendship that looking back, probably saved my life. I chatted in Discord servers, I made my first ever fan art and even a few viral memes, and I laughed and I cried at the beautiful things other fans made. I met countless people who loved Dragon Age as much as I did, and some of them have even become real-world friends. Among them are a handful of DA devs whose names made me so proud to see in the Veilguard credits that I cried. Watching the death of the franchise and now the closure of the studio alongside them has been heartbreaking.

What I think is remarkable is that my experience is far from extraordinary: BioWare had a way of writing stories that made people feel seen and could bring them together, and most crucially, could do so for people who didn’t necessarily fit into the “typical” gamer community. While this chapter is over, its impact is not, and I know the many creative people impacted by layoffs and now the studio closure will go on to make more beautiful, uniting things. I can’t wait to see them. â Steph Rideout, BioWare fan

My wife and I came together because of Mass Effect. We were friends who realized we had this thing in common and somewhere between the game’s shared language and sharing our headcanons about our Shepards’ exploits, we fell in love. We’ve been together for over 12 years and married for six. Earlier this year, we planned a week-long vacation with friends we’d also made through Mass Effect and Dragon Age, last month we finally had the trip happen. People from all across the States from different backgrounds came together to be geeky friends in person. All because we each loved the stories BioWare told us and made connections through that. We’re already planning for next year. â Erminia, Community Manager

I’ve been a fan of BioWare games for almost 17 years. I was introduced to Mass Effect in 2010 in the basement of my new friend Joe’s house. He, another new friend Caitlin, and I started hanging out in Caitlin’s mom’s basement shortly thereafter. I watched the two of them play Mass Effect and would occasionally grab the controller and work on my own Shepard.

In 2014 they introduced me to Dragon Age: Inquisition and that’s what made me buy an Xbox One (which I still have and still play these games on!). I hadn’t gamed much since middle school but loved Inquisition and replayed the Mass Effect games. Both series influenced who I am as aÂ  34 year old. I cosplay Shepard and the Warden and have plans to make more costumes. I am an archivist who does their best to uplift marginalized voices and makes sure history is told how it happened (despite what Varric may try to add). I value my community and what makes each person in it unique and amazing.

I was a bridal party person for Joe and Caitlin, who got married on N7 day in 2020. They are still two of my closest friends and I cannot imagine our 20s without BioWare, especially Mass Effect. â Taz, BioWare fan

BioWareâs games are often lauded for their character work, difficult choices, and revelatory story moments. But which of the studioâs games was the very best in this regard depends on who you ask.

When I first played Dragon Age: Origins, I was a young queer person that had only very recently come to terms with my orientation and identityâjust a gayby!! I think Iâd heard that there was romance in the game, but I had no idea about the inclusion of gay romance in it. When I first came across same-gender romance content in the game, I was stunned. Iâd literally never experienced anything like it in a game before. It had never even crossed my mind before that this could be a thing, that this was possible. It seriously blew my mind. To see this in such a way, in a medium you love, the hero of a story; it was so meaningful and moving that I cried at the computer. Iâll always remember that. Thatâs when I knew [BioWare would be important to me]. â Felassan, BioWare fan, content creator, and blogger

I’m not interested in relitigating *everything* about [Mass Effect 3âs] ending after all these years. But to cut to the chase: I loved it, because after three games of saving the world, it was the first time I felt a protagonist was tired. Not that I was bored with the game. Not that combat had become rote. Just that Shepard was *exhausted* from saving the world.

And when she got to her final glory, no, it wasn’t some cutscene cavalcade of sins remembered flashing before my eyes. Before they even added the extended endings, I remember sitting there, thinking of what kind of universe Shepard would never get to see. And, seemingly unlike the rest of the internet, I was content. â Justin Clark, games media

The introduction of Steve Cortez. I think that was still my first experience with a game that gave me [a gay romance] option, and certainly the first one that wasn’t giving that option in a way that stank of “oh look at how progressive we are being, aren’t we amazing?!” At the time it was at least a year before gay marriage became legal in the UK, and so it felt significant. Since then BioWare has been a studio that I associate with telling stories over trying to fit in with what the rest of the AAA competition was doing at the time. â Gabe Titchiner, BioWare fan

I played Mass Effect for the first time when I was a teenager. Things weren’t great at home. I had just come out as a lesbian and my family didn’t accept it. Playing through an incredibly well-written sapphic romance spanning three whole games gave me a sense of belonging at a crucial time in my life. Commander Shepard became my role model. I found the Mass Effect community online and developed friendships in it that have lasted over a decade. Those games and the friendships I found through them changed me forever. â Sage, BioWare fan

I think [what impressed me the most] was how Dragon Age II subverted the expectation of player agency. This wasnât Mass Effect, or Origins, or KOTOR where the right selection of choices could save the world. Your world was going to hell no matter what. You just got to choose what kind of person you wanted to be while your life burned down around you.

The game thereby became an altogether more intimate tale of a found family caught in the tide of history. The cast of violent, sexually fluid weirdos remains one of the all-time great RPG parties, and the deeply cursed city of Kirkwall is an all-time great fantasy setting. With a narrative that spans years, you get to feel like you havenât just gone on adventure: youâve built a life for yourself and your friends. When you must choose who to side with at the end of the game, whether to side with the inevitability of authority or with the chaos of rebellion, that moment carries a weight that most RPGs canât match, precisely because the game has spent its efforts investing you in the characters and the setting, not just the plot.

I donât give a good goddamn what people say about it: for my money, Dragon Age II is one of the greatest video games ever made. It challenged my beliefs about what made a good narrative, and that made me a better author and critic. â Saoirse Stone BioWare fan, critic, author, Editor-In-Chief at Stone Freedom

The twist in KotOR was my âI am your father.â It completely got me and Iâve been trying to replicate that feeling for almost my whole life. â Eric Perez, BioWare fan

The Revealâ¢ in KOTOR is legendary, but even outside that, you could already see that this studio was special in the way it could build a universe for you. I love you. Top five video game jokes of all time. â Chase Wheatley, BioWare fan

The moment in BG1 that I stepped outside of Candlekeep in the prologue was just… It was a moment I’ll never forget. For the first time, I was THERE. And seconds later when Elminster arrived with his classic red attire and the line “Ho there, wanderer…”, that has created a moment that has stayed with me for almost 30 years. â Phil Morgan, host of Deleted Saves Podcast

I remember the first time I played through Mass Effect as a teenager, and feeling the floor dropping out from under me.
