#3662. EA Just Shelved A Mysterious Sims Project—That Could Be Good News For Players

It's been another rough year for video games, with countless studio closures, staff layoffs, and projects that barely managed to even get off the ground before they were unceremoniously cut short. But things are feeling especially grim after EA trotted out two beloved franchises--Mass Effect and Dragon Age--for what amounted to a public execution via the announcement that BioWare has been shuttered. 

This was especially painful for Mass Effect players, who were looking forward to the upcoming Mass Effect 5, which we now know was tentatively titled Mass Effect: Universe. But it's not just BioWare fans who are upset at the moment. Fans of EA's other properties are growing increasingly concerned about the future of those franchises, if any future is planned for them at all. My colleague Levi Winslow recently wrote about their concerns for the Skate franchise in the wake of layoffs at its development studio. Meanwhile, I'm quite worried about the fate of The Sims.

In the same breath it announced the end of BioWare, EA also reaffirmed its commitment to Apex Legends, Skate, and The Sims franchises. But everyone knows that when it comes to profits, EA's sports titles outrun its other IPs by a country mile. If EA is willing to pull the plug on legacy franchises like Mass Effect and Dragon Age, where does that leave its other franchises, like The Sims 4?

According to EA, Sims fans need not worry, as the company is committed to "focusing on the long-term potential of The Sims." Apparently, focusing on that long-term potential involves shelving a project The Sims team has been working on for years: Project Rene, AKA Project Lotus, AKA the nebulous next entry in The Sims franchise, which appears to be some kind of weird Sims MMO mobile game thing. Instead, EA will be focusing on Project Evergreen, which is rumored to be a sort of remaster of The Sims 4, with all (or most) DLC packs included, and recurring bugs squashed.

"We're supporting this franchise by pausing work on one of the next titles in this franchise" doesn't exactly inspire confidence, especially after the nonchalance with which EA just killed two other beloved game franchises. But I think this actually might be the right move. 

It's been a bumpy couple of years for The Sims, and many players aren't particularly enthused about Project Rene/Lotus, as it seems to be once again trying to recreate The Sims Online, something EA has tried to rebuild over and over. In fact, much of the reason The Sims 4 launched in such awful shape was due to the fact that it was initially meant to be an MMO-style game that could run on mobile devices. Less than a year before launch, EA pivoted to a more traditional Sims game--but by then, so much of the game had been built with online play and mobile devices in mind that it was too late to turn back. Despite releasing over 100 DLC packs and embarking on a concentrated campaign to squash the game's many, many, many bugs, longtime Sims players are still frustrated with the state of The Sims 4, often pointing out the numerous ways it pales in comparison to its predecessor, The Sims 3. 

The Sims 4 is officially "done" in that there are no plans to release any more expansion packs for the game. When it comes to the future of the franchise, most players don't want the next Sims title to be yet another attempt at shoehorning online and/or mobile gameplay into a game that is, at its core, all about building and playing with digital dolls in their digital dollhouses. So EA's decision to hit pause on Project Rene/Lotus's development isn't something I find especially heartbreaking. In fact, I think it's the first truly wise decision EA's made regarding the franchise in a long time, provided EA actually plans to support Project Evergreen long-term (which the name Evergreen would suggest).

Sims 4 players don't want Project Rene, but they do want either The Sims 5 or a complete, playable version of The Sims 4--ideally one that doesn't require the purchase of $1,600 in DLC packs to feel "finished." Hitting pause on its weird, experimental Sims projects in favor of attempting to preserve The Sims 4 in a stable, playable, "evergreen" state is arguably the best decision EA could make, given the current state of both EA and The Sims franchise. Pouring resources into a concept that has failed before (online MMO-style Sims gameplay) rather than a tried-and-true formula (a digital dollhouse) would only harm the franchise at this point.

Of course, there's no telling what kind of shape Project Evergreen will launch in, assuming it does successfully make it to launch. It sounds like the Evergreen devs have a deadline to hit--hence the reshuffling of resources away from Rene/Lotus--but even with the increase in development resources, there's no guarantee Evergreen will be a massive hit with players.

Provided the rest of development does go smoothly and Evergreen is indeed well-received by players, it may still fall short of EA's goals when it comes to profits. EA has spent the last decade doing everything possible to monetize the living hell out of The Sims 4, a game that--unlike EA's lucrative sports catalog--is largely intended to be a solitary gaming experience that doesn't require online play. Back in the olden days of The Sims 1, 2, and 3, players would purchase the base game, a few expansion packs, and maybe a couple of "stuff packs" for extra decor options, but that was all one really needed to enjoy the game. 

The Sims 4, however, introduced an era of seemingly endless DLC: expansion packs, game packs, stuff packs, kits--there are over 100 of them, ranging in cost from $40 to $5, and totaling around $1,600 if purchased individually outside of sales and bundles. In addition to the constant stream of DLC releases, EA has in recent years implemented daily login rewards, various events and challenges, and even a paid mod store nobody asked for--all in the hopes of getting players to spend more time and money on The Sims 4. For a while there, I half-expected EA to implement a Sims 4 battle pass.

There's no telling what sort of irritating monetization tactics we'll see in Project Evergreen, but at the very least, Evergreen sounds like an attempt to try and maintain the series' roots, rather than continue chasing the mobile MMO Roblox-like direction Project Lotus seemed to be taking. Even better, Evergreen may turn out to be the game Sims players have been aching for since The Sims 4 launched to middling reviews back in 2014: a game that isn't fundamentally broken and lacking in content.

The real question is if Evergreen will be successful enough to keep The Sims franchise alive. Given that EA's new owners were happy to kill off what was shaping up to be a potentially great Mass Effect game, it's not hard to imagine a world where the Grim Reaper inevitably comes for The Sims, regardless of whether players love or hate Project Evergreen. After all, feelings don't generate dollar signs, and EA's new owners have made one thing abundantly clear: killing off an iconic franchise is "worth it" if it saves EA a few Simoleons.

It's clear Julia Stiles is on the elimination bubble of Dancing With The Stars, after guest judge Shirley Ballas gave her a 4 on Halloween Night. While there's always a chance for competitors to bounce back after an off week, I think her song choice for Disney Night is only going to help her get sent home this week.

The song list for Disney Night dropped ahead of the annual episode on the 2026 TV schedule, and there are some questionable picks. Julia and Ezra Sosa's choice might be the strangest of them all, because I think plenty of fans will have something to say about a Hamilton song slipping through.

I know that Disney loves to remind us that Hamilton is available to stream with a Disney+ subscription, but it is not a stage production that originated from the House of Mouse. I'm sure that's why Julia and Ezra were allowed to pick "Satisfied" for their upcoming performance, but that doesn't make it any less aggravating.

There are too many good Disney movies to include a song from a project that doesn't originate from the studio. While it's true that contestants and pros have limited control over the songs they get during a season via a questionnaire, clearly that had to fill out something that ranked it high on the list to get it. Is Dancing With The Stars' Disney night just another vehicle for the company to cross-promote its other brands? Absolutely, but including a dance number for something that isn't inherently from it really kills the vibe.

It feels like the writing is on the wall for Julia Stiles on Dancing With The Stars. Now that viewers have seen her pay homage to Save The Last Dance as well as her tribute to Heath Ledger, they're now more concerned about her actual dancing.

I'm Watching Dancing With The Stars For The First Time, And Now I Am All In

Stiles had a standout performance with her contemporary dance and scored all nines. That said, when it comes to more traditional dances, she's struggled tremendously and hovered toward the bottom of the leaderboard most of the competition.

With the exception of Tatyana Ali, the rest of the Dancing With The Stars contestants are leaps and bounds ahead of her. Just from talking to various people who are watching this season, there seems to be a growing desire to keep Tatyana in the competition and let Julia's run come to an end.

We're deep into DWTS Season 35, so it's inevitable that favorites are going to go home. Only the best of the best should be in the finale, and if they aren't, the audience and judges have failed. As such, I think it's curtains for Julia this week, unless she puts on a truly stellar performance.

Disney Night is on ABC and Disney+ on November 2nd. Make note of the fact that it's a Monday night, as network television will be taken over by the midterm election results.

#3658. Gang Of Dragon Won’t Be The First Game From Nagoshi Studio. It Won’t Be Any Game At All

Nagoshi Studio, the studio formed by Yakuza creator Toshiro Nagoshi at NetEase, has been shut down before it even released its first game. According to Gematsu, shareholders officially dissolved the developer on October 31 via a resolution later published in the Japanese government gazette Kanpo.

Under Nagoshi, the studio worked on Gang of Dragon, a new game that looked similar to the veteran developer's work on Sega's Yakuza and Like a Dragon series at Ryu Ga Gotoku Studio. Work on the game continued over the years, and a trailer was shown at The Game Awards last year, but in March, reports said NetEase had pulled its funding for the project. The official Gang of Dragon YouTube channel also went down for a brief time in April, and in May, the game's website was whacked.

So why did the studio shut down? Exact details on the reasoning behind its closure haven't been revealed yet, but in March, Bloomberg reported that Nagoshi was seeking another $44 million to get Gang of Dragon across the finish line, a figure NetEase may have decided wasn't worth investing in further.

Meanwhile, Nagoshi's former home, RGG Studio, has released multiple games since he left. Nagoshi's final credits with Sega were for Lost Judgment, Super Monkey Ball Banana Mania, and Virtua Fighter 5: Ultimate Showdown; since then, RGG Studio has released five games in the Yakuza/Like a Dragon franchise. These include prequels, sequels, and remakes: Like a Dragon: Ishin, Gaiden: The Man Who Erased His Name, Like a Dragon: Infinite Wealth, Gaiden: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii, and Yakuza Kiwami 3 & Dark Ties.

Next year will see the launch of Stranger Than Heaven, described as a distant prequel to Like a Dragon that spans 50 years.

I don’t know what’s going on with the Survivor edit. I’m not saying fans can always tell who is going to win halfway through every season, but typically at this point, there are two or three strong contenders who more educated fans have coalesced around. That’s definitely not the case at this point in 51. Everyone is still all over the island with their predictions, and there’s perhaps no better example of that than Kristin Flickinger.

Arguably the most universally liked contestant on 51 with the possible exception of Ori, Kristin has probably gotten the most consistently positive edit of any player. Every single time she’s on the screen, the editors seem invested in making her look good. We got a segment where she showed off her negotiation skills. We got a segment where we saw her winning over her tribemates after the swap. We’ve gotten multiple segments where she showed off her literal survival skills. We’ve gotten confessionals where she’s detailed all the strong relationships she has on the island. We even got a montage of all of her audition tapes over the years.

It’s the kind of edit Survivor players dream about getting, but is it a winner’s edit? Well, fans and so-called Edgic experts are not on the same page at all. Some see her as overwhelmingly the most likely winner, and some see her as very likely to be eliminated deep into the merge but very explicitly prior to the endgame. Let’s talk out both sides.

The case for Kristin as a winner is pretty clear and many in the community are making it, perhaps most prominently RHAP’s Shannon Guss. No one on the show has gotten more consistently positive content, and you could argue that a few times, the show even distorted the truth to make her content even more positive. For example, she was shown dunking on Kilby during the negotiation, even though anecdotal evidence later told us she didn’t necessarily get better supplies. That’s been a recurring theme. Even the negativity she’s gotten, which has mostly been from Maggie confessionals, has framed her more as dangerous than incompetent or annoying.

If you dig a little deeper, however, there is actually some cause for concern with Kristin’s edit. Many in the community think she’s being framed as a fan favorite we’re supposed to be sad about exiting the game deep into the merge, and there’s definitely some evidence for that. First, while she’s been a consistent part of the show, there are actually seven players who have more confessionals than her at this point in the game: Devin, Jelly, Lewis, Kilby, Brady, Ori and Erik. She’s only middle of the pack among the players who are left, and that’s actually really bad considering she was picked for negotiation, went to exile island, got swap screwed and got prominently injured during an episode.

Given all the plot-relevant moments she’s been involved in, it’s actually kind of weird she hasn’t gotten more content, which is probably because it keeps getting cut. An emotional scene between her and the Survivor doctor where she was informed she would be allowed to stay in the game got cut and released as an online exclusive. Another scene from this past episode where she explained what happened on Exile Island to her tribe got cut and also released as an online exclusive. Given she’s only in the middle of the pack on content, if she were the winner, it kind of feels like the show would find reasons to use her, not cut compelling scenes she’s involved in.

To me, the most likely scenario is probably that she gets taken out in the 5 to 7 range. That’s typically the point in the game where all the remaining players work together to eliminate the people they think are most likely to win a jury vote, and as a strong public speaker with great relationships, a compelling backstory and a passion for the game, Kristin screams jury threat. There’s also the pesky issue of fire hanging over her head too. We’ve been repeatedly shown and the other players have repeatedly seen her making fire very quickly. She’s the type of player you have to eliminate before the final four, which is why that range just outside makes so much sense.

I have no idea who is going to win this season (though I can guess who is going to lose) and by extension, I have no idea where Kristin is going to finish. All I know for sure is that she’s delightful, and the editors clearly want us to have positive feelings about her, whether she's the possible host Jeff Probst was referring to or not. Maybe that’s because she’s going to go on and win the whole thing, or maybe that’s because she’s the emotional gut punch we’re going to get when she’s betrayed by other players who are worried she’ll win the jury vote if she gets there.

#3656. Take This Step Now to Avoid Being Locked Out of Your Spotify Family Account

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you are on a Spotify Family plan, you may need to verify your location to keep your account active. Like many streaming services, Spotify is cracking down on family sharing for users who don't live in the same household by requiring QR code verification for some plan members—and once prompted, you must verify within seven days or risk being locked out of Family and Duo plans for a full year.

Spotify does require users on shared plans to verify their address when they join to confirm that they live with the plan manager and to re-verify if the manager changes addresses. Users may also be prompted via to re-enter their full address if Spotify "can't confirm" their location. This obviously doesn't prevent users from sharing plans, as Spotify isn't actually tracking your location but rather cross-checking addresses.

Some users may start seeing a QR code verification requirement, which has stricter parameters and may be more difficult to get around if plan members aren't in the same location. In these cases, the plan manager must open a QR code on their phone via Profile > Your Premium > Manage, and plan members must scan it with the camera on their phone.

According to Spotify's support page, both users must be in the same location to complete the scan, and the QR code changes every few seconds, making it hard to send screenshots to anyone not present in person. However, as 9to5Google notes, some users have been able to work around these restrictions with video calls, using multiple devices to complete the scans.

If you are prompted to complete location verification either by email or QR code, make sure you do it within seven days of the notification—otherwise you'll be lose access and be downgraded to a free plan. Spotify says that you can rejoin the same Family or Duo plan again, but you'll be restricted from joining a different shared plan for a full year.

#3653. Inside Gatcombe Park, Princess Anne’s Beloved 730-Acre Country Estate

On any given day at Gatcombe Park, Princess Anne’s sprawling 730-acre privately owned estate in Gloucestershire, one might spy the 76-year-old checking in on her prized Highland cows, a scarf tied firmly over her famous bouffant. At the estate’s cutting-edge stables, her daughter, Zara Tindall, may be riding with her daughter and nieces, coaching them as they jump through courses designed by her father Mark Phillips. Meanwhile, Zara’s husband, rugby star Mike Tindall, may be playing beer pong in the “party barn” with his brother-in-law Peter Phillips, while Princess Anne’s husband Sir Timothy Laurence watches rugby in the cozy, cluttered parlor of the estate’s main Georgian mansion.

The scene is that of an idyllic country estate, a beloved family home that is also a working farm. It may also serve as an example to Prince Harry and Meghan Markle as they search for their own private estate in the British countryside. “Being able to take on a place like this—for me, I’ve got to make it work,” Princess Anne once said. “This is not something that comes free, this has got to pay its way, otherwise I can’t stay here."

Since the ’70s, Gatcombe Park has been Princess Anne’s place of refuge from endless royal duties, a place to live the country life she loves. “Every year, month and day, I realise how fortunate and privileged I am to have grown up and spent most of my life in the countryside,” she told Country Life in 2020. “It’s not only the space, appreciating the seasons, the wildlife, the plant life, the arable crops and the livestock, but, most importantly, it’s the people who live and work there and understand the complexity of their environment.”

The estate was the perfect wedding present from the late Queen Elizabeth to her athletic, no-nonsense daughter and her first husband, Mark Phillips. The two Olympic equestrians first met at a party in 1968, although the meeting was not auspicious. “We had to be told that we’d met in 1968 before we remembered,” Anne recalled.

Zara Phillips riding her horse Toytown at Gatcombe Horse Trials, with Princess Anne and Tim Laurence, September 16, 2001.

They later reconnected and found they shared many things, including an obsession with nature, country life, and the world of elite equestrian competitions. “Anne couldn’t marry her horse, so she’s marrying Mark,” the then Prince Charles reportedly joked about his future brother-in-law. Princess Anne approached their upcoming wedding with the same stoicism she did everything. When asked if their relationship could withstand the pressure of publicity and public duties, the Princess was blunt. “Can? It’s got to, hasn’t it.”

The two were married on November 14, 1973, in a lavish ceremony at Westminster Abbey. From the start, Phillips, an active captain in 1st The Queen’s Dragoon Guards, proved to be cut from a different cloth. He refused all the Queen’s offers of titles and was not popular with some royals and their courtiers, with the protective Prince Charles reportedly nicknaming him “fog,” because he was “so thick, according to Kitty Kelley’s The Royals.” British journalist Auberon Waugh (the eldest son of novelist Evelyn Waugh) was even more brutal. He unkindly described him as “Princess Anne’s grinning, speechless husband, who, if you whistle at him, wets himself.”

The entrance hall with a stone floor and decorative pillars, June 1976.

In spite of naysayers, the couple forged ahead and began searching for the perfect country estate (“I’ve never been a city girl,” Anne noted). In 1976, former Home Secretary Lord Rab Butler, suggested the couple check out Gatcombe Estate, his family home outside of the village of Minchinhampton.

The estate featured over 700 acres of woods and cultivated farmland, stables, a fine herd of Hereford-Friesian cattle and a trout lake, “netting an income of between 14,000 and 18,000 pounds a year.” The five-bedroom neoclassical main house, built with Cotswold stone, was originally built in 1774. In 1820, the famous economist Davis Ricardo had the house redesigned. The exterior was covered in roses and wisteria, and the couple were instantly smitten. The interior was not as picturesque, with one friend describing it as “rather dreary, in some disrepair, with suspicions of dry rot.”

But the couple loved it. “We stood on the front steps and looked out at the view; it was quiet, it was secluded, it was peaceful with woods down each side of a long valley,” Phillips recalled. “I thought to myself—well, whatever is inside, we can change, given time. But this we can never change. This is just what we have been looking for.”

Peter Phillips, age 9, on horseback at Gatcombe Park, July 28, 1987.

A week later, Princess Anne took Queen Elizabeth to view the property. In June 1976, it was announced the Queen had purchased the home for the couple for a reported 500,000 to 750,000 pounds at the time. Workers on the estate suggested to reporters that Anne could help on a tractor. “Since the Princess can drive a tank, why not?” one quipped.

There was immediate backlash to the private purchase. “When members of the Labour Party government heard that the Queen was buying her daughter and son-in-law the farm and woodland property at such a price, left-wing members called for the introduction of a wealth tax,” the Australian Woman’s Weekly reported. “They pointed out that last year Parliament voted the royal family an extra $600,000 to help it pay its bills.”

MP Willie Hamilton took it a step further. “They’re gold-plated parasites. The lot of them. All parasites.”

For their part, the palace was tight-lipped, claiming the purchase was “an absolutely private matter.” Lord Butler also scoffed at the reported price, claiming it was not nearly as high.

Ignoring the noise, the couple began working to improve their new estate, insisting they would pay their own way. “People never believe me when I say that we’re just like any other young married couple with a mortgage,” Phillips said. Princess Anne did indeed drive a tractor, and Prince Andrew and Prince Edward were said to come down to help during harvest season. While his wife stayed at her apartment working in Buckingham Palace in London during the week, Phillips worked tirelessly on the farm, “so tired that I fell asleep in front of the television.”

Making good on their dream to turn Gatcombe into an A+ equestrian facility, the couple in 1983 hosted the inaugural Gatcombe Park Festival of British Eventing. The event became a mainstay on the elite equestrian calendar. Held every August, it featured Olympians competing in cross-county (courses often designed by Phillips), jumping and dressage events. Thousands attended the televised program each year, and many more visited at the annual craft fairs and the Gatcombe Food Festival.

Princess Anne with her bull terrier dogs at the British Horse Trials Championships, August 31, 1996.

Phillips found many ways to monetize the estate, even turning brushwood cleared from the courses into paintbrushes. Meanwhile, the couple raised their children Peter and Zara at Gatcombe, where life revolved around horses. “One enjoys riding, but when you get back there’s still half a day’s work to do just to keep the darn things on four legs,” Anne noted, per The Princess Royal by Helen Cathcart. “You have time for nothing else.”

Tindall has noted that she had an “amazing” country childhood on the estate, far from the hustle and bustle of royal life. “It was a great place to grow up around horses, looking after animals—the respect and partnership that you have to build with the animals, it teaches you so much you know growing up and as a kid,” she said.

But this didn’t mean that growing up on the farm wasn’t hard work. The Phillips children (whose parents declined for them to have titles) were expected to carry their weight. “We had to do everything with them,” Zara recalled. “We had to clean our tack. We had to muck them out.”

Zara, who eventually became an Olympic rider herself, recalled that her parents had very different ways of training. “Mum’s very relaxed. She’s like, Just, you know, just do what you do, whereas my father’s like, More of this, more of that, she said. “My father was quite critical... Very rarely you would get a, Yeah, that was good, out of him. So it was always striving to try and get that comment. He was a tough coach.”

There was also tension inside the home. Both Princess Anne and Phillips were unfaithful (Phillips even had a daughter, Felicity, with a New Zealand woman in 1985) and in 1989 they separated. But Phillips did not go far, moving to Aston Farm on the estate and continuing to run Gatcombe’s events (he finally left Aston Farm in 2013). Princess Anne stayed in the main house with her new husband, Sir Timothy Laurence, who she married in 1992.

According to those who have visited the main house, life there is surprisingly “unroyal” and laid-back, filled with bric-a-brac and cozy, worn decor. “Journalists and biographers who visit Gatcombe for the first time are still struck by the informality of the place,” Anne’s biographer Nicholas Courtney told Glocester Live. Gatcombe Park has become a true family compound, with Peter Phillips and his family reportedly having a cottage there. Zara and Mike Tindall have raised their children at Aston Farm since 2013.

Running the estate has also become a family affair. Peter Phillips helped organize the annual Gatcombe Park Festival of British Eventing in later years. Princess Anne would present trophies and Zara would compete, as photographers took pictures of Anne’s grandchildren frolicking.

Zara Phillips, Mia Tindall, and Princess Anne at the Whatley Manor Horse Trials, Gatcombe Park, September 8, 2017.

Farming operations have also continued, a practice Anne clearly relishes. “I have lived at Gatcombe for more than 42 years,” Anne wrote in Country Life in 2020. “We were not looking for a farm, but it has been a real privilege to try to work with what we have. Ours is an organic, extensive grass enterprise, usually complicated by running the horse-trial championships in early August. The woodland is a real mix of trees—mostly beeches, but huge numbers of ash of all ages. Who knows how many will survive, but I feel the naturally selected mix could be an important part of the answer.”

That same year, the official royal website also noted the extensive livestock on the property that included 230 Wiltshire Horn sheep, 14 White Park cows, 6 Highland cows, and 2 Gloucester Old Spot sows. There is also a prized herd of rare Suffolk Punch horses, which Anne is passionate about saving. The estate also includes a kitted out party barn, which includes catering facilities, large screens and bar/lounge areas.

The last few years have been eventful, in both good and bad ways. In 2021, Zara gave birth to her third child, Lucas, on the bathroom floor at Aston Farm. In 2023, the estate hosted their last Eventing Festival, citing rising costs and COVID as the reason.

“The horse trials at Gatcombe and more recently the Festival of British Eventing have been a major part of my life for over 40 years when The Princess Royal and I first had the dream,” Mark Phillips said in a statement at the time. “It’s truly a great sadness that the original model and indeed the sport has changed so much. Since COVID, costs, particularly insurance, have risen so much that the numbers no longer add up. It is an end of an era, the next 40 years of the sport will be different, let’s hope it can be equally special.”

In 2024, Princess Anne was reportedly injured by a horse on the property, which resulted in her being hospitalized for a concussion. But there was happier news in June of 2026, when Peter Phillips and his new wife Harriet Sperling reportedly celebrated their wedding reception at the party barn.

Although Princess Anne still continues with her punishing schedule of official engagements, staying in her London apartment in St. James Palace when she must, it is clear her heart lies at Gatcombe Park, surrounded by her loved ones, beloved animals and the crisp country air. “It’s very normal; there isn’t any standing on ceremony, and she’s the only one with a title,” royal historian Robert Hardman told Hello!. “She’s a very good grandmother. She’s hands-on, but like all grandchildren, I think they can get away with things. She dotes on them.”

In fact, the normally tight-lipped Anne has said so herself. “It’s really nice to come back and just be yourself in an area like this.” Former royal courtier Ailsa Anderson agrees. “Gatcombe is her bolthole, where she is not the Princess Royal—she is Anne.”

With filming set to resume soon on Prime Video's God of War series, 55-year-old actor Dave Bautista revealed in an Instagram Story that he's packed on a beefy 20 pounds of muscle for the role of Kratos, bringing his weight to 250 pounds. #3650. Beware of These iPhone Duo Preorder Scams

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

iPhone Duo preorders officially launched last week to high demand, a quick sellout, and delayed delivery estimates. Naturally, scammers are finding ways to capitalize on the rush to obtain Apple's new foldable, so if you're in the market for a new device, be on the lookout for signs of compromise.

Soon after the iPhone Duo was announced, threat actors jumped into action, setting up fake preorder pages that looked like Apple's official website but were actually designed to deliver a malicious payloads to your device. As Malwarebytes outlined in late September, these pages promised a $500 voucher and AppleCare+ coverage in exchange for your contact information. But submitting the form isn't actually the scam. Rather, simply opening the page launches the attack, which uses the DarkSword exploit chain to bypass iPhone protections and gain access to cryptocurrency wallets, messages, contacts, emails, calendar entries, and location data.

This scam began several weeks ago and seemed to specifically target iPhones running iOS 18.4 to 18.6.2. Apple has said that devices running the latest versions of iOS 15 to 26 are protected from the exploit, so if your iPhone is up to date, you are likely at minimal risk for this specific scheme. That said, beware of websites and social media posts that promise access to the iPhone Duo faster or cheaper than other sources, as this is almost certainly a scam designed to steal your information or install malware on your device. Official sources for preorders include Apple itself (through the official Apple website or Apple Store app) as well as major cell carriers.

Another scam to be on the lookout for involves fraudulent charges for an iPhone Duo you didn't order. News outlets in Hong Kong have reported that shoppers are seeing transactions from Apple appear on their bank and credit card statements—even when they haven't actually tried to buy the device since preorders went live. This may be the work of bad actors who have harvested credit card details via phishing or data leaks and are using them for fraudulent purchases.

While this specific scheme doesn't appear to be widespread (yet), you should check your financial statements and accounts regularly anyway given how vulnerable your data are to theft and fraud. If you see a charge you don't recognize or duplicate charges, report it to your bank or card issuer immediately using contact information from a trusted app or client portal.

Scammers will also take the threat of fraudulent charges one step further: They may contact you directly about supposedly suspicious transactions and claim they can help resolve the issue if you provide personal information or account credentials. With the iPhone Duo specifically, bad actors may also call pretending to be Apple or a carrier and ask you to confirm information about your order, possibly to avoid having it canceled. As always, any communication that provokes fear and a sense of urgency should raise red flags. If you're not sure who you're talking to, hang up and call back directly to confirm.

Every Halloween, I think I've seen the year's best celebrity costume, and then somebody comes along and changes my mind. And while there's plenty keeping me entertained on the 2026 TV schedule, former Riverdale stars Madelaine Petsch and Camila Mendes just gave me a fictional show I'd absolutely watch. Petsch and Mendes spent Halloween dressed as Wilma Flintstone and Betty Rubble, respectively, and their ridiculously glamorous photo shoot has me wishing The Real Housewives of Bedrock were an actual series I could binge.

Petsch and Mendes shared the pictures in a joint Instagram post on Halloween, captioning them "The Real Housewives of Bedrock," complete with a bone emoji. Amber Asaly shot the photos, and they look like promotional stills for the most unhinged Bravo spinoff imaginable. Prehistoric sets, dramatic side-eyes, and enough attitude suggest somebody's about to get kicked out of the Bedrock country club. Seriously, take a look:

A post shared by Madelaine Petsch (@madelame)

Since Andy Cohen recently teased the possibility of more Real Housewives cities, I think somebody should put Bedrock on the list. Seriously, who’s Flintmobile’s stone log rollers do I gotta buff to get this thing greenlit?

Petsch nails Wilma's signature look: red curls piled high, a white one-shoulder dress with a jagged hem, and those enormous pearls. Mendes, meanwhile, makes a fantastic Betty in a blue dress, matching hair bow and sleek dark bob. They've kept the recognizable Flintstones details while giving everything a glossy, fashion-editorial makeover. I'd genuinely love to see the rest of their imaginary cast.

The photos are where the joke really takes off. In one, Betty leans over to whisper something into Wilma's ear, while Wilma looks appropriately scandalized. Another pic shows them posing with champagne glasses, and there are shots of the pair lounging among rocky scenery lifted from the cartoon. They even brought two little white dogs into the mix. I'm not sure what the dogs have to do with prehistoric suburbia, I suppose its hard to secure a tiny dino on short notice, so I’m glad the pups got an invite.

As much as I love the outfits, someone in the Instagram comments deserves a gold star for the funniest response to the entire shoot. User @herecomesjoey wrote:

RIP CW, you would’ve greenlit this show by Monday morning 😭👌🏽🔥😍

I've always had a soft spot for how the 1994 live-action Flintstones movie brought Bedrock to life, and these costumes have that same wonderfully ridiculous attention to detail. Only this time, Wilma and Betty look ready for a Bravo reunion special.

They don’t really produce their own original series anymore, but the CW is still on the air, and I laughed harder than I probably should have. Considering these two spent seven seasons on Riverdale, a show that got increasingly bizarre right up through its series finale, a CW-style Flintstones drama feels almost plausible. I can already hear the trailer voice-over: "In Bedrock, everybody has something to hide."

Of course, Petsch and Mendes have a history of taking Halloween costumes very seriously. Just last year, they dressed as Kim Possible and Shego, proving that transforming into beloved cartoon characters is becoming something of an annual tradition for these two. Before that, they joined fellow Riverdale alum Lili Reinhart to dress as the Gotham City Sirens for Halloween, after previously transforming into the Sanderson sisters from Hocus Pocus. This year's costume is a duo rather than a trio, but Reinhart still showed up in the comments with a perfect one-word endorsement: "Icons." I can't argue with her.

What really sells these pictures for me is how completely the actresses commit to the bit. They look ready to feud over a dinner-party seating chart carved into a stone tablet. Unfortunately, The Real Housewives of Bedrock isn't a real series. For now, it's an excellent Halloween photo shoot and another reminder that Petsch and Mendes know how to have fun together long after Riverdale ended. But if anybody wants to commission a pilot, I expect a reunion special hosted by a particularly exhausted Fred Flintstone.

Riverdale is streaming in its entirety with a Netflix subscription.

#3647. Little Shop of Horrors: An Oral History

Like an unassuming plant from outer space, Little Shop of Horrors had humble beginnings—but managed to blossom at a surprising rate. The musical is performed numerous times each year across the globe; the current Off Broadway production has been running for seven years straight. But none of that would have happened without the 1986 film version of Little Shop, a cult classic that Warner Bros. executives once characterized as “the highest-budget musical they’d ever done,” according to its director, Frank Oz. “I don’t know if it’s true or if it’s hyperbole, but that’s what they told me to pressure me into doing a good job.”

“I love it. Audiences love it,” says composer Alan Menken. “Anytime I watch Little Shop,” though, “every other second I’ll be thinking about my late collaborator”—lyricist, book writer, and original stage director Howard Ashman, whom he worked with on both the original stage show and the film. “I’ll look at his work and how amazing it is,” Menken says. “Then people come running up to me, and I go, ‘It’s Howard.’”

Moranis as Seymour Krelborn and Ellen Greene as Audrey in Frank Oz's 1986 film adaptation.

It’s been nearly 40 years since Audrey II began its cinematic rampage. To commemorate the movie—which is getting a brand-new 4K restoration and rerelease on Blu-ray—Vanity Fair spoke with Oz, Menken, producer David Geffen, stars Rick Moranis, Ellen Greene, Tisha Campbell, Tichina Arnold, Michelle Weeks, and more about assembling an A-list cast including Steve Martin and Bill Murray; the film’s long, difficult production; why Moranis had to film several of his scenes as though he was moving in slow motion; and the movie’s elaborate, expensive, utterly depressing original ending.

Back in 1959, legendary low-budget filmmaker Roger Corman had a challenge: to shoot an entire film in two days. He enlisted Charles B. Griffith to write a film using preexisting sets—including a florist shop and a dental office. The original Little Shop of Horrors was born: a scrappy but ambitious B movie featuring a brief cameo by a young Jack Nicholson.

The film became a staple of late-night television, entrancing viewers like a teenage Howard Ashman. As an adult, Ashman knew it’d make a great musical. His agent watched the Corman film and told Ashman he was out of his mind.

Poster for the TV adaptation of The Little Shop of Horrors, 1960.

Ashman then approached jingle writer Alan Menken about doing the musical with him at the WPA Theatre, of which Ashman was a cofounder.

ALAN MENKEN (COMPOSER): I thought it was absolutely amazing. This was one of those so-bad-it’s-good movies. When we first took a crack [at writing the songs], it was actually very close to the Corman film…. And then Howard said, “You know, I think we should do this as the dark side of Grease.”

You think about those beach blanket horror movies from the early ’60s or late ’50s, and there is both a tackiness and an incredible exuberance about them at the same time. And then you think about the Phil Spector Wall of Sound and his work with the Ronettes. So the score became a whole homage to all those early rock influences, and it just became a perfect tonal bed for the storytelling.

ELLEN GREENE (“AUDREY,” ORIGINAL OFF BROADWAY AND THE 1986 FILM): I got to watch Howard direct several sessions with Alan playing on the piano. They counterbalanced each other; Howard was very serious, and Alan is just a sweetheart. Although Howard was also a sweetheart.

MENKEN: What makes for a good collaboration, first of all, is to get your fucking egos out of the room. Bring your talent into the room and always be ready to throw something out…. Don’t ever allow yourself to fall in love with your own work. You are driving this particular thing called a musical. Howard was the best I ever experienced at doing that…. Howard knew exactly what he wanted.

GREENE: I remember walking down the street [listening to a demo of the song “Skid Row” and thinking], I don’t want to do a camp musical. [Then I] got too unemployed, and I'm listening to “Somewhere That’s Green.” I started quietly singing “Green” to myself, and it made me cry. And I knew right then and there I had an Audrey inside of me that was waiting to be born…. When I went into the audition, I did the scenes, and the speaking voice just came out of me.

Michelle Weeks, Tisha Campbell, and Tichina Arnold as Chiffon, Crystal, and Ronette, respectively, in the 1986 adaptation.

LEE WILKOF (“SEYMOUR,” ORIGINAL OFF BROADWAY): I got a call from a casting director that I knew in New York. [She said], “A theater in New York is doing a musical based on the movie Little Shop of Horrors…. Would you come in and read for the part of the dentist? I walked into the audition…and Howard Ashman looked at me and he went, “You’re not a dentist. Would you mind going out and looking at the role of Seymour?” And I did, and I got a callback. Apparently, it was between me and another actor. His name’s Nathan Lane. And the assistant director apparently said that she thought that I would work better as a Seymour. Her name’s Connie Grappo, and we’ve been married 42 years.

GREENE: I was a brunette at the time. I said, “Howie, meet me at 14th Street.”… And I tried on a long blonde wig with bangs, and he went, “I don’t know what you’re doing.” I said, “Just let me finish.” Paul Holmes, the stage manager, helped me cut the wig, and Howard still wasn’t sure. Then I completed the look [with a black cocktail dress], and he loved it.

The show opened at the WPA in 1982 for what was supposed to be a two-week “showcase,” with the actors all making a mere $50 a week in exchange for being reviewed by major theater critics. It was an immediate success.

WILKOF: It was impossible to get a ticket. It went from being this obscure little show. The word on the street apparently grew.

MENKEN: We had lines of producers around the block.

DAVID GEFFEN (PRODUCER): I don’t quite remember how I first got involved, but I think Cameron Mackintosh and I were approached…. I thought it was terrific.

Director of photography Robert Paynter on set, 1986.

MENKEN: We knew there were people who wanted to bring Little Shop to Broadway, and Howard said absolutely not.

GEFFEN: The [Off Broadway] show was very successful, highly thought of. Then we opened it up in Los Angeles. It was natural that we’d make it as a movie.

The creative team began planning a feature film, which Geffen would produce. Tom Cruise, per Menken, wanted to play Seymour (although his reps have claimed he wasn’t interested in the role); he was immediately vetoed by Ashman. Geffen had his eyes set instead on a comedic actor from Canada.

RICK MORANIS (“SEYMOUR”): I first started hearing about the film being made early on, like ’82 or ’83. I ran into David Geffen randomly—I had never met him before—and he stopped me and said, “I want you in my movie.” I said, “Which one?” And he told me, and I said, “Well, okay!” And then for the next three years, I would occasionally hear about it or read about it in the hands of one director or another, and nothing ever happened.

At one point, Steven Spielberg was slated to produce the film, with Martin Scorsese directing. John Landis was also attached to the project for a time. Perhaps the name that made the most sense on paper was Frank Oz, best known as the man who brought to life childhood staples like Miss Piggy, Fozzie Bear, and Yoda.

FRANK OZ (DIRECTOR): I saw [the show] and thought it was amazing. But I didn’t have a take on it. And when I read the script for the movie, I couldn’t get my hands around it. It was so big, and I didn’t have a clear vision of it. So, through my agents, I said, “Thank you, but I can’t do it.” Two weeks later, something clicked in me regarding the three girl-group singers. I realized that when they entered onstage, all they could do was enter from the left or from the right…. But in a movie, it’s 360 degrees; you can have them enter from anywhere. So that’s what kind of changed my idea. I called back and I said, “You know, I may have a way to do this,” and then David asked me to do a rewrite…. Then I went to London, and I spent a month on the rewrite, and I felt really good about it. I knew if I said yes [to directing it], that’d mean two years of my life would be on this project. But I was committed and excited about it.

GREENE: [Frank] has to see the vision. Until he sees the vision in his mind’s eye, in his head, he will not take something on.

Greene, Steve Martin as Orin Scrivello, and Moranis, 1986.

MORANIS: [It’s] the intersection of so many skills and qualities that he has: a remarkable sense of humor, a real affinity for the darker arts and all the puppeteering, and such a keen eye for design.

OZ: I had not known Rick, who is now one of my closest friends after all these years. I never knew Rick, never heard of him because I was in London shooting for five years, and Rick was doing SCTV, and that was not shown in London. But I saw some of his work and I thought it was brilliant.

MORANIS: I knew this was an extraordinary opportunity to do a musical, and shoot it in London, and work with Frank and that cast. [Film] musicals don’t come along too often for people who get to call themselves actors.

OZ: David understandably wanted a star, but…I couldn’t see an Audrey with the depth and the heart that was given to the character by Ellen. I couldn’t see that being done by anyone else. So I asked him to please let me do a screen test with Ellen, and he did. And that’s when David said yes to Ellen.

MORANIS: Ellen had created the character of Audrey for the Off Broadway show many years before we did the movie.  She wasn’t just acting the part of Audrey; she was Audrey. I had just come from years of comedic character acting on SCTV and in films like Strange Brew and Ghostbusters. So we were both approaching our performances for Little Shop in similar ways. I think that’s why we had such a strong onscreen chemistry.

GREENE: Frank saw the character a little more heroine-like [than she was onstage]. He wasn’t sure about the “Audrey-isms,” and so that’s why the line “You don’t meet nice boys when you live on Skid Row, Mr. Mushnik” is not in the film…. Freddy Cooper was a cameraman…and he’s the reason I got to do the squeak in the film. Frank and Rick weren’t sure, and he spoke up and said, “Sir, I think it’s funny.”

OZ: David also suggested Steve Martin, and Steve I had worked with a little bit prior to that. Steve and I talked, and at the time there was a very popular character called Fonzie, and Steve said he just didn’t want to do Fonzie. I said, “Absolutely, that’s fine.” He wanted it more like Elvis. I said, “Fantastic.” As far as I was concerned, Steve could do anything.

The film’s glue wasn’t any of its big names; it was the three girls, all under 18, who made up its ’60s-girl-group-esque Greek chorus.

TISHA CAMPBELL (“CHIFFON”): I had just auditioned to play Regina King’s best friend in 227, and I didn’t get it. So I quit. I was 16 years old. I wanted to go to camp with my friends. And while I was there, my mother called me. She said, “Your agent keeps bugging me. They won’t stop calling me.” I said, “Did you tell them I quit?” And she said, “I told them and said you just wanted to be a regular kid, and they were like, ‘Please, just this one audition. Then you can go to camp.’ Can you just do it and I’ll send you right back to camp? No harm, no foul.” And I was like, “Okay, fine.”

MICHELLE WEEKS (“RONETTE”): At the time, I was on Broadway doing Tap Dance Kid, and I had a management company submit me. When I went for the audition…I was like, Yeah, they’re not gonna pick me. I’m too big. But then when we went for the callbacks, I was like, Oh, I have a chance!

Steve Ross, Courtney Sale, Steven Spielberg, and David Geffen at an off-Broadway performance of Little Shop of Horrors, 1982.

TICHINA ARNOLD (“CRYSTAL”): [I was] starting off in the theater [as] a little kid with wide eyes and ready to get it cracking. I just so happened to know Michelle Weeks because she and I went to school together. We had the same friends, and then Tisha and I knew each other from just auditioning.

CAMPBELL: They auditioned girls from everywhere…. And it just so happened that [the three girls cast were] from the tristate area. Michelle was from Brooklyn, Tichina was from Queens, and I was from New Jersey.

ARNOLD: And Frank Oz, we asked him, “How did you choose us?” And he was just like, “You girls had a synergy.”

Little Shop presented a real technical challenge: how to capture chemistry between its lead, Rick Moranis, and the man-eating plant. For the voice of the plant—named Audrey II by Seymour—the creative team turned to Motown singer Levi Stubbs. But actually bringing the creature to life would be the real struggle.

OZ: There’s only two words necessary, and that’s [puppeteer] Lyle Conway. Lyle passed recently, sadly, but Lyle is the one responsible for the plant. He was a pure artist, and he did an incredible job.

BRIAN HENSON (PRINCIPAL PUPPETEER): I think [Lyle] brought almost everybody that was on Return to Oz, and then a lot more because it was a much bigger build…. My dad [Jim Henson] came and visited the shoot a couple times, for sure. And then my little sister, Heather, was in it. She’s in the dentist scene.

BRAN FERREN (SPECIAL VISUAL EFFECTS): Lyle Conway was brilliant, his vision for how to create—because there wasn’t one plant; there were a series of plants that were used to show its various stages of growth.

OZ: I needed pure lip sync, really good lip sync, not just a mouth opening and closing. Because you’re on film, they can see in a tight shot that it’s just a puppet if it’s just opening and closing.

HENSON: This was definitely the biggest and the most complex [thing] that had ever been done in animatronics. It was also before the Creature Shop–type people were using motors, so it was almost all cable-driven.

OZ: All the performers had to rehearse the song over and over and over to make sure they hit every single syllable.

HENSON: There’s no eyes on that character, so it was always going to be the physical presence of the plant combined with this mouth and this voice. So Levi’s recordings were very important to Frank. [But] we started rehearsing before he even had Levi’s recordings.

MORANIS: They were looking for ways to make vowels and consonants so that they could form words, and then form phrases, and then be able to do that to music. And it was only possible to do at a slower motion than 24 frames a second.

There are 24 still frames in every second of standard film. But during rehearsals, it was discovered that the plant could not believably lip-synch at that speed. The production’s solution was to slow down Audrey II’s motions—operating the plant at 12 frames per second, then speeding the film up later so that it would look normal. This meant that anytime Moranis was in the same shot as the plant, he also had to move, act, and sing in slow motion.

MORANIS: The trick was to keep my butt tight. Because we keep our butt tight when we’re walking quickly. And when you try and walk slowly, it’s very easy to let your butt relax. If you were to look at that at 24 frames, you would look like you were doing some sort of weird walk. So by keeping the butt tight, I managed to pull it off, I think.

GREENE: [Frank] taught me how to act at 12 frames per second. He put me in a room; he had a camera. He said, “Ellen, walk across the floor.” He set it up to the regular speed. He said, “Now look at this,” and it looked like I was rocking back and forth. He showed me how you have to walk only forward, and ballet sort of helped. I worked on acting, talking, and moving in 12 frames a second.

John Candy as Wink Wilkinson and Moranis as Seymour Krelborn, 1986.

FERREN: How do you put emotion into a plant? I mean, news flash: It wasn’t a real man-eating plant! And my suspicion is that not many people watching the movie said, “Oh my God, they found an actual man-eating plant.” If you get it right, they shouldn’t be thinking about that.

HENSON: When we started rehearsing, we just had a bit of skin for the lips. The head was bald, and it was quite lightweight. Every week they’d build a little bit more, and it would just get heavier and heavier and heavier. By the end, it weighed more than 150 pounds.

With the cast—and plant—in place, filming began on October 21, 1985, at Pinewood Studios on the 007 Stage. Per Frank Oz’s vision, it had to be done entirely on a soundstage, as the world they were creating couldn’t come to life on location.

OZ: Roy Walker, our brilliant production designer, and I walked through the whole set. I told him where I felt things needed to be for each particular number, because I had planned the numbers in my head months before I even got to London.

GREENE: [As] someone who first was on this tiny, tiny stage, [I walked] into Pinewood Studios…and there in front of me is the land that is built, that I only saw in my mind's eye because I was on the stage—and it’s even better than I ever imagined.

OZ: My goal was to make it a movie sensibility instead of only a theatrical sensibility. It’s really a mixture of it, and my real goal was to make sure it reflected the gritty atmosphere of an Off Broadway play, and not a musical. I didn’t want to make it into Hello, Dolly! or Mame.

MENKEN: Little Shop is meant to be this tacky show in a hole-in-the-wall…and they wanted the film to have that same quality.

OZ: The opening number is packed with information. You have the three girls dancing in the streets. I needed people to know that they were not regular human beings, so I had them sing in the rain—and they were not affected by the rain.

ARNOLD: Frank Oz explained to us, “It’s gonna be raining around you, but you won’t get wet.” And I was like, “How is that gonna happen?” He showed us the pipes and stuff that they had in the ceiling and said, “Okay, so choreography-wise, you’re gonna follow this path [to ensure you don’t get wet].”

CAMPBELL: Man, it was raining on our heads! The first time we filmed that scene, it was raining so hard that you could tell on our faces. They had to cut. They were like, “You can’t show that it’s raining on y’all!”

WEEKS: We had to be up early in the morning, and us being teenagers, we were going places we weren’t supposed to go, like the club. We used to go to the Hippodrome and get out at like two or three in the morning, and have to be at the studio at six. But it was so much fun!

OZ: I loved shooting “Suddenly Seymour.” When Roy showed me the set—which is beautiful—I saw that staircase that he made. I thought, Okay, it’s got to be a Romeo-and-Juliet section where she’s up there, and he’s down there, and he runs up there. So it was all built up to that moment. I had him run up the stairs 30 to 40 times.

GREENE: Fifty-three takes we had to go up those stairs. [The “Suddenly Seymour”] set was so beautiful, with grass growing through the cracks and bricks and cobblestones. If any set was ever called a work of art, I think this would be applicable.

CAMPBELL: [Steve Martin] was very quiet off camera. But when that camera rolled, I was just in awe of how he would light up and become this character, and just be very big and broad.

OZ: When David suggested Billy [Murray, who has a cameo in the dentist scene]—and I knew Billy before that—I called him. I said, “Hey, Billy, do you want to do this?” And Bill said, “Do I have to do the words?” And I said, “No. I don’t care what words you use as long as you’re the masochist and he’s the sadist. That’s all I care about.”

As technical as the film itself was, nothing could compare to the plant.

OZ: People tend to think, Oh, puppets, that’s no problem. They are the hardest things in the world to shoot, to do right…. Just “Feed Me” alone took five weeks to shoot.

HENSON: Nowadays, you think of a film unit shooting 30 to 40 setups a day. Little Shop of Horrors was way down at three to five, five to seven if you were shooting easier stuff. It was slow, meticulous shooting. And Frank is a very meticulous director.

OZ: We’d usually go about 25 to 30 takes to make it perfect.

MORANIS: [For] “Feed Me,” Brian was inside the head of the plant, and then all the other puppeteers were connected to the plant. The actual plant store that we shot in was constructed on the second floor, and the first floor is where the puppeteers set up camp and where their cables would go down to. They would have monitors, and they could watch themselves operate the plant.

HENSON: There were vines that were being worked by one or two people on each vine. It [took] maybe five of us to work the head…. With “Mean Green Mother”…there’d be puppeteers all the way around the outside of the set, doing cables, and on the roof of the set was another maybe 10 puppeteers. And the set was also on top of a tank, so they could get to the underside of the pot for the roots.

MORANIS: It was so enjoyable to do [“Feed Me”]. I don’t think I had a moment when I didn’t enjoy shooting it. I do remember one aspect, just because it went on for so long: Every day I would come in and put on the same clothes.[Just] put on the same clothes every day for five weeks, or whatever it was.

HENSON: [During “Feed Me”], I’m right there. I said to Lyle, “You know, I just can’t stay hidden all the time.”… I couldn’t hide completely behind the stem. And Lyle said, “Okay, this is what we’re going to do. You’re going to wear a skintight green Lycra suit, and I’m gonna glue leaves to it.” There’s bits of me in the shots, but you don’t know it’s me.

The stage version of Little Shop ends with the plant eating Audrey, Seymour, and, finally, the audience. The filmmakers were determined to capture that same spirit, and did so in a $5 million epic ending that saw Audrey II taking over New York—ending on top of the Statue of Liberty.

OZ: Before I even went to London, I was at David Geffen’s office, and David said to us, “You know, you can’t end it the way the play ends it, because you’re killing your leads.” And Howard and I both said, “Well, we want to be true to the ending from Off Broadway, in part because we just like being true to things, but also because it was a deal with the devil. He deserved to die because he killed people, even though he didn’t do it maliciously.”

GREENE: I gravitate to the dark underpinnings of the Faustian tale. Even though there's a magical world full of whimsy and silliness and goofiness, it has a moral with dark underpinnings.

OZ: Richard Conway had worked about nine months on the models of the destruction at the end. It was no CGI, no opticals. Richard had built all this stuff, and then built the small plant that would be on the bridge, and he did an incredible job having the plants like Godzilla raging through the city.

MORANIS: I remember that, when I saw the ending of the play, something was off with it, but it didn’t matter because the vines came out of the ceiling. And I thought, This is brilliant! They’re distracting you from the tragic ending by creating this fun experience of stuff flying out of the ceiling.You’re part of the action. The shock and surprise, and all the tactile fuzziness of it, distracted from whatever was lacking in a fulfilling happy ending. It didn’t occur to me that that would become a problem in the film.

This is Audrey II in Little Shop of Horrors, 1986.

GREENE: In the play, I say a line—“When I die, which should be very shortly…”—just to lighten the moment, and it’s silly. It releases some of the energy in the audience. But when I say it in the film, it’s very intimate, and it’s to Seymour. It’s weighted differently…. I’m very proud of that scene.

MENKEN: When we did [the first] preview…I'm sitting there going, “Wow! Look at this!” I look at David Geffen, and he said, “Yeah, wow, but wait a second—the cards, Alan!”

Those would be the reaction cards on which that era’s preview audiences would answer questions regarding how much they liked a film. Typically, producers were looking for 55% of a screening’s viewers to say they’d “recommend” the film. Little Shop’s first screening in San Jose got 13%. Oz asked Geffen to screen it again in LA to make sure this wasn’t an anomaly. The results were the same.

GEFFEN: People were hostile to the end of the film. They were hostile to the characters getting killed. We thought we were going to have a disaster.

OZ: The audience was against me because I killed people they loved, and it was a great lesson to learn. Onstage, they also die, but the actors come out for a bow. In movies, you don’t come out for a bow. You just die.

GREENE: [Onstage], my death is not as heartbreaking. It's a mixture. Just when you’re about to laugh, I’ll make you cry. Just when you’re about to cry, I’ll make you laugh.

GEFFEN: I think what the audience didn’t get was that this was a send-up of monster movies in the ’50s. They took it quite seriously. We made it so realistic that they were horrified by the end of the movie.

FERREN: The idea was, I want to go out smiling and happy. Now, I guess, it shows my personality. I went out smiling and happy, watching the world end.

OZ: They wouldn’t even release the movie if I didn’t change the ending…. The hardest of all was the terrible, terrible, terrible phone call I had to make after Richard Conway and his amazing crew made all those miniatures in that whole ending. I remember I had to call London from Los Angeles and say, “Richard, we’re not going to use any of it.”

What I also heard at the time [after the failed test screenings] was that there was a thought to try and get Rodney Dangerfield to do the voice of the plant, I assume to make it funny. My intent for the plant was to have it [be] a strong antagonist. If it was funny, there would have been no threat to Seymour or Audrey.

The team had to figure out a new finale that would stay true to the story and give Seymour and Audrey a happy ending. The solution? Seymour would electrocute the plant during their final showdown, and he and Audrey would finally get to move somewhere that’s green. But sitting outside of their dream home would be a small Audrey II, smiling at the camera.

OZ: The idea [came together] very fast. Howard and I knew exactly what had to happen. That part where the little plant smiles at the end was because I couldn’t make it a happy ending. It had to have some danger to it…. We went back [to London] for a month to reshoot.

Made on a budget of $25 million, including $5 million that wound up on the cutting-room floor, the film was unleashed on the public on December 19, 1986. It wound up doubling its budget at the box office, earning $54 million globally. A modest success, it didn’t necessarily set the world on fire—at least, not right away.

ARNOLD: Tisha and I had a really interesting moment. We decided to go see the movie in Times Square. We sat behind these two girls that were watching it, and we were like, “Okay, let’s go in when it’s dark so nobody recognizes us.”

CAMPBELL: There were these three girls sitting behind us. And [during the movie], they were like, “I’m so sick of these girls popping up out of nowhere!” [Laughs] So our first experience being able to watch our film, there were some haters behind us.

ARNOLD: Needless to say, I don’t watch myself anymore.

MENKEN: “Mean Green Mother” was nominated for the Academy Award, which was just amazing. I remember Levi Stubbs came out and sang “Mean Green Mother.” And I'm thinking, Wow! Well, I have a speech in my pocket. Who knows? Howard just goes, “Alan, you can relax. You’re not giving any speeches tonight.”

OZ: [When it came to home video], that’s when everything kind of exploded.

GREENE: [While currently touring with the movie], I get to see their love of Little Shop, their love of Audrey, even their love of me. I just hug everybody because I know they want it.

WEEKS: I went to see [Ellen on the tour recently]. It brought me to tears a couple of times…. They introduced me, and Ellen was surprised to see me. I was so happy to see her. We hugged and everything, and we talked a bit later on. But the warm reception that I got kind of brought me to tears because they were like, “Oh my gosh, it’s Ronette!” It just made me feel seen.

ARNOLD: I always said Little Shop of Horrors was a movie done before its time. But it stood the test of time and is still standing.

MENKEN: It is a true musical, and it’s driven by high-energy pop and rock, and it’s not about, “Oh, look how hip it is.”… It’s a thrill ride that really moves fast.

GEFFEN: I thought it was a terrific movie when we made it. I was very unhappy that we changed the ending…. I always wanted to restore it. And, as you know, we did. [In 2017 a version of the movie with the original ending played in theaters.]

OZ: I finally got to call Richard before he retired, saying, “Richard, finally they’re going to see your work.”

MORANIS: It’s become a point of discussion for people, whether they prefer one to the other, or if they’ve seen both of them. It’s prompted a couple of extra releases of different versions of the film.

OZ: I think [it resonates] because when you look at the movie, you know it’s not CGI…. It’s nice to show people what could be done when a lot of human beings get together and make something.

#3646. Resident Evil Director Reacts To Backlash: “I Should Have Known Better”

Resident Evil is a huge success at the box office, recently surpassing $400 million globally. It's also received fantastic review scores. But hardcore fans of the game series took issue with the film and its direction because it did not contain any storylines or characters from the source material. Director Zach Cregger never intended to, instead opting for his own original story that is set in the world of Resident Evil. Now, Cregger has spoken more about the fallout, saying he became "frustrated at the conversation" around his movie and specifically how it "didn't have anything to do with the movie."

He said on The Town that the conversation from the hardcore Resident Evil fanbase was that the movie didn't live up to their standards, even though Cregger never said he was trying to make a movie that did that.

He said he really loves and is proud of the movie he made. At the same time, Cregger admitted, "I should have known better" about how fans of the game series might react. Anyone who has been on the internet and engaged with anything related to gaming knows how intense hardcore gaming fans can be about even the seemingly smallest of issues, but Cregger said he overlooked this for reasons he doesn't fully understand.

"I should have understood that that was going to be the case," Cregger said about the blowback. Cregger previously said he was naive to think gamers would embrace him and his idea for the Resident Evil movie.

Cregger previously said he would never make another franchise movie after Resident Evil, but he's softened somewhat, saying on the podcast that he has a "never say never" attitude about it. Asked if Cregger's anti-franchise stance might limit his job opportunities in the future, Cregger said that after Barbarian and Weapons, he feels like he is "playing with house money."

Cregger said he's basically already won in life and the rest of his career is gravy. He said he goes into his projects now thinking it could be the last film he ever makes, and he's OK with that. "I'm going to swing for the f**king fences," he said. "I'm going to pour it all out to make this as good as I am capable of making it. And whatever happens, whether it makes a lot of money or no money, I just have to make sure I left it all on the court. And if that's the end, then I've had an amazing run."

Cregger is, of course, not finished making movies. His next film is the deep space sci-fi movie The Flood, starring Jennifer Lawrence. He said in the interview that it's his biggest-budget movie ever; previously, that record belonged to Resident Evil (a reported $75 million before marketing costs). Cregger said he shouldn't admit this publicly, but he believes there are real benefits to making movies on lower budgets, in part so a filmmaker like himself has to get creative as he works against constraints.

The Resident Evil movies are produced by Constantin Films, which bought the rights back in the '90s and has retained them ever since. After Welcome to Raccoon City flopped, Constantin planned to put the film franchise on ice ... until Cregger showed up with a pitch.

In addition to The Flood, Cregger is producing the next Weapons movie, which is the spin-off, Aunt Gladys.

#3644. Why Your Smartwatch Size Really Does Matter

“Is my watch too big?” is a constant question on forums dedicated to smartwatches and fitness trackers of all kinds. (Some, but fewer, wonder if their watch is too small.) Personally, I don’t much care how a watch looks, but I’ve noticed that size can make a big difference in how accurately a watch functions. If your watch is too big, your numbers may be off.

Watches measure heart rate through an optical sensor on the back of the watch. (That’s what you see glowing green back there.) The heart rate sensor detects how that light reflects off the blood vessels in your skin. To get a proper reading, it needs to be snug against your skin, ideally in a way that blocks out ambient light.

If the sensor loses contact with your skin, or if too much light sneaks in, heart rate readings may be inaccurate. If a watch fits you well to start with, you can generally get an accurate heart rate by simply making sure the watch is snug during workouts.

But if a watch is too big, it can move around, letting light in. When you run, if a watch is bouncing around, the sensor may detect a flash of light with every footstep. This can lead to your watch reporting a heart rate that is the same as your cadence (footsteps per minute), which is sometimes called “cadence lock.” Some runners will cover their watch with a sleeve (especially in cold weather) to minimize this possibility.

No matter how you wear it, a big watch on a small wrist is likely to have a lot more difficulty than one that fits properly. Very small devices can have a similar problem: The device isn’t large enough or can’t be tightened enough to block light. This isn’t usually a problem with wristwatches, but it may explain why smart rings tend to be so poor at daytime heart rate tracking.

Now, is this a real-life concern, or just a theoretical quibble? I wasn’t sure, until I took the Forerunner 265 and 265S for a run at the same time. These are the same watch, with the same heart rate sensor, differing only in size. You can read about my results here, but the graph tells the story pretty well: The smaller 265S (42 mm) captured my heart rate more accurately than the 265 (46 mm).

If heart rate accuracy were the only issue, I would tell you to get the smallest watch you can find. It wouldn’t even look weird; before smartwatches became popular, wristwatches were often much smaller than a person’s wrist. (Watch old movies and you’ll see some tiny watches, even on people who don’t have tiny wrists.)

But watches are big and seem to be getting bigger. A bigger screen means numbers, text, and icons are easier to read. This is great news if your vision isn’t the best anymore, or if you use the watch while exercising and want to be able to see what’s on your screen with a quick glance.

Bigger watches can provide bigger screens, but also bigger batteries and more room for other internals. This is probably at least partly why more “premium” watches come in bigger sizes. That said, it’s hard for me to distinguish when a watch is huge because it needs room to pack in its hardware features, versus when the company is making the watch bigger so it will seem fancier and thus justify a higher price.

And this brings me to something I need to rant about. Smartwatch and fitness watch companies know that watch size matters: They often offer two sizes for at least some of their models. The Apple Watch Series 12 comes in 42 or 46 millimeters, while the Garmin Forerunner 570 comes in 42 or 47 millimeters, to give a couple of examples.

But when it comes to premium models, those options often disappear. The Garmin Forerunner 970, far more feature-rich than the 570, only comes in a 47-millimeter size, matching the larger size of the 570 but without a smaller option. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 only comes in a 49-millimeter size, which is even larger than the larger size of the Series 12. I’m about to start testing a Hyrox feature that only comes on Amazfit’s Balance 3 or Balance Ultra watches; those watches are 51 and 52 millimeters, respectively. This is getting ridiculous.

As a woman reporting on tech, I can’t ignore the way gender plays into this. According to ANSUR II, a U.S. Army study, women have an average wrist size of 154 millimeters (about 6.1 inches), and men have an average wrist size of 176 mm (about 6.9 inches). My wrists are right around 6 inches, making me very average for a woman.

When companies make two sizes of watch, the smaller size usually fits the average woman’s wrist fairly well, and the larger size is a better fit for men’s wrists. This isn’t a perfect match, of course, since plenty of women may fit or prefer the larger size, and vice versa. I’m glad the companies market these as “small” and “large” or just by the numerical size.

But as a person with six-inch wrists, I can’t wear a large watch without dealing with bouncing, rubbing, and potentially inaccurate data. I’m no twig; I’m perfectly average for my half of the population. But those larger watches just aren’t going to be as accurate for me as they are for the average man. I noticed a similar phenomenon when I tested the heart rate tracking in Powerbeats Pro 2 earbuds: They barely worked for me, but did fine when I tried them on a man with larger ears.

There's also an uncomfortable intersection between this gender dynamic and the way watch companies use size as a signifier of how fancy a watch is supposed to be. While Garmin only offers the 970 in a large size (47 mm), they only offer the cheaper 70 and 170 in smaller sizes (both 43 mm). Garmin’s Venu 4 comes in both 41 and 45 millimeter sizes, but the cheaper Vivoactive 6 is only available in 42. Having a small wrist can save you money, but it still shuts you off from some of the more premium options out there.

For my work reviewing and testing watches for Lifehacker, I’ve worn smartwatches ranging from around 40 millimeters (an older Apple Watch) up to 48 millimeters (a tie between the Kospet Tank and the Amazfit T-Rex 3 Pro). I love a watch in the 40-42 millimeter range; I can tolerate one around 46 millimeters if it’s lightweight enough that it doesn’t bounce too much; and I really have a hard time with anything larger.

Those bigger watches are hard to snug up sufficiently for a workout; get them tight enough not to bounce, and they’ll feel like you’re nearly cutting off your circulation. After a long run with a big, heavy watch, I’ve sometimes gotten red, irritated spots on my wrist from the inevitable friction. You may not be able to judge how badly a watch will fit when it's still in the box, but I do have a rule of thumb for when you try it on.

To judge visually, I find it helps to put a watch on your wrist, rest your arm on a table, and look directly down at it. If the lugs of the watch extend past your wrist, it’s too big. You want the watch to fit on your wrist, not overhang the sides.

And if you prefer a watch size that isn’t going to be the most accurate for heart rate, remember that you can always pair a chest strap to a watch that supports it, or to your phone if you don’t have a compatible watch. If you prefer a larger watch for more readable text or maps, or if you want a premium feature that doesn’t come in smaller sizes, a chest strap may be the way to get the best of both worlds.
