#3622. Is Ken Paxton’s Senate Campaign in Texas the Bitter End of Trumpism?

At Coyote Crossing Saloon, a smoke-filled dive bar off Interstate 37, a 64-year-old Texas native named Tracey was showing me his teeth. He’s missing about half of them—a casualty, he said, of toothpicks soaked in horse liniment that serve as a potent stimulant for truckers looking to stay up late on long-haul drives. Tracey is a big fan of President Donald Trump. He voted for him three times and still supports him, even after all the excesses of his second term. But he can’t stomach Ken Paxton.

Dragging on a cigarette, he pointed to the Texas attorney general and Republican Senate candidate’s alleged corruption, his reputed infidelity, and the case of a plea deal his office offered to a Waco man charged with sexually abusing a young boy. “Just because you have all this money, how are you gonna just do as you please and nobody’s gonna say nothing?” Tracey remains a fan of the state’s Republican governor, Greg Abbott. “He’ll win, so I’m happy about that.” But Paxton? “Get him out of there.”

Texas attorney general Ken Paxton embarked on a bus tour of the Lone Star State as his Senate campaign draws to a close.

If Paxton has lost voters like Tracey, Republicans might be in trouble. Texas hasn’t sent a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, and this seat could determine who will control Congress for the final two years of Trump’s presidency. Yet the collapse of Trump’s approval across the country has put even red states like Texas in play for Democrats, creating a powerful undercurrent that Paxton’s opponent, James Talarico, has surfed to a narrow but steady lead in the polls. That’s turned Texas into a money pit: $500 million has been blown on advertising already, thanks in part to at least $168 million pumped into the state by Elon Musk, and it’s on track to be the most expensive Senate race in history.

It didn’t have to be this difficult. Since 2002, the seat has been occupied by Senator John Cornyn, who ran for reelection with the backing of the Republican establishment and a sizable war chest. But in the primary, the president backed Paxton, a scandal-plagued culture warrior who went above and beyond Trump’s loyalty tests, while Cornyn drew suspicion that he was fair-weather MAGA. Now Trump has placed a risky bet. These midterms are a referendum on the president, but this race, more than any other, is a gauge of his movement: Can a candidate with many of Trump’s failings but little of his charisma careen into the United States Senate?

Even in the ruby-red counties of West Texas, Trump’s support is slipping. Will Paxton pay for it?

A crowd in Sherman, Texas, settles down into movie theater recliners to watch Paxton speak.

This is the final sprint of the Paxton campaign, a frenetic bus odyssey dubbed the Come and Take It Tour. (There’s a cannon printed on the side of the bus.) The voyage has swept through the border towns of McAllen and Laredo, up through exurbs like Selma—just outside San Antonio—on to Austin and Waco and Dallas, then out through hundreds of miles of high plains to the West Texas towns of Amarillo and Lubbock, and then down to Corpus Christi for a rally with Trump himself.

“The person that is without sin, please cast the first stone,” said Pastor Ruben Mendez in his opening prayer at Paxton’s campaign event in Selma. The room was silent. “I don’t think so. I don’t think there’s anybody that can do that.” Mendez, the pastor of Iglesia Shalom, a small nondenominational church tucked down an alleyway in a suburb nearby, was speaking to a crowd crammed into the Blue Bonnet Palace, a country music venue in a corrugated iron barn just off the highway. A cardboard cutout of Brooks & Dunn hung above the stage alongside a motionless disco ball.

Paxton is locked in a close race with James Talarico, whom Trump has nicknamed “Talafreako.”

The pastor’s reminder that “King David was a flawed man” was met with scattered applause. If the subtext of this homily wasn’t clear enough, a protester soon made it explicit. “Why were you in Dubai?” a young man yelled as Paxton took the stage. He was swiftly bounced by security to chants of “USA!” from the faithful.

The protester was referencing the latest chapter of the biblical Paxton oppo file. The Wall Street Journal reported that Paxton spent New Year’s Eve 2024 partying in Dubai with Tracy Duhon, his rumored mistress, as well as two men who were then fugitives from US justice, one of whom had donated to Paxton. This indiscretion joins a long list of scandals that supporters of Paxton are willing to overlook to back the candidate (and, perhaps more importantly, keep Texas red). On the tour, they often invoked faith to make their case.

House Republican Darrell Issa, who served as chairman of the House Oversight Committee and worked with Paxton when he was a crusading state attorney general, stumped for the candidate on his swing from San Antonio to Georgetown. When I asked why he felt compelled to campaign for Paxton given the baggage, Issa echoed Pastor Mendez.

The line was lengthy to get into the rally in Corpus Christi.

“Is President Trump a man without flaws? No. But neither was Andy Jackson, neither was Bill Clinton, neither was Abraham Lincoln,” the congressman said. “So you judge somebody in elected office based on the honor that they bring to the office, the energy they bring, and the initiatives that they’re involved in, and that’s where [Paxton] excels. So am I going to say that this is somebody that, like our savior, was without sin? No. But I’m not somebody without sin, and neither are any of the voters.”

Some would argue that Paxton’s sins are more exotic than those of your ordinary Texan. He was charged with two counts of felony securities fraud by Texas prosecutors and in 2024 reached a deal to avoid trial that involved paying nearly $300,000 in restitution. Separately, the Texas House impeached him in 2023 on charges of bribery, corruption, and abusing his office. (Paxton has denied the allegations that led to his impeachment.) With state legislators under intense pressure from Trump, he was acquitted by the Senate. “Yes, it is true that my intervention through TRUTH SOCIAL saved Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton from going down,” Trump boasted afterward.

There’s also Paxton’s reputation for jet-setting: In his 11 years as attorney general, an Associated Press investigation found, Paxton spent an extraordinary amount of time traveling to plush locales including “California wine country, Caribbean resorts, and European tourism hot spots.” It cost the taxpayers at least $1.9 million to cover the expenses of his security detail. And then there was, of course, the 2013 surveillance video that caught Paxton pocketing a man’s $1,000 Montblanc pen. (His campaign called the incident a “mix-up,” and Paxton returned the pen after he was contacted by a sheriff’s deputy.)

Even some of the ads supporting him carry a bit of a shrug. Angela Paxton, who is suing her husband for divorce on “biblical grounds,” which is King James for “cheating,” appears in a spot urging Texans to vote Republican down the ticket. “Let’s talk about the elephant in the room,” she says at the start of the ad, which ends without any further mention of the elephant.

For many in the Republican establishment, these indiscretions have pushed Paxton beyond the pale, but that’s of little concern to the nominee’s supporters. “He may not have his life together,” said Janet, a Paxton backer from Corpus Christi, “but he’s better than the alternative.”

There was strong turnout for a Trump rally to support Paxton in Corpus Christi.

Kevin, a 62-year-old from the San Antonio suburbs, brought his wife to see Paxton speak in Selma. “I believe in this country there is a battle between good and evil,” he said. “I try to judge characters in a biblical sense.” Where does that leave Paxton, a man accused of violating quite a few of the commandments? “I’m okay with Ken Paxton,” Kevin said, waving a hand as I ran down the list of transgressions. “I believe Trump is the best president we’ve ever had. And we got to have people in there to support him.”

Jason Norton, 50, a bearded and tattooed pastor at King’s Trail Cowboy Church who delivered the prayer at Paxton’s stop north of Dallas, had a similarly permissive view of his alleged infidelity. “Christian does not mean perfect. Nobody would approve of that. And I’m sure he probably regrets it. But what he did hurt himself and his family. What Talarico’s doing will hurt the entire state.”

In a quaint historic town north of Fort Worth, I met Steve Bannon at the Texas headquarters of his War Room podcast. A longtime Paxton backer, Bannon has spent much of this campaign season in the state, broadcasting to the Trump base while helping to advise the Republican’s campaign. “We have not seen the data yet that shows part of our coalition actually coming out and voting against Trump,” Bannon told me. “I think most of them are staying home. That’s a huge win for us. If they come out and vote against us, we’re fucked.”

After Musk dumped $168 million into the race, Republican super PACs pumped out ads casting Talarico as too extreme for Texas. The Democrat’s disposition as a love-thy-trans-neighbor seminarian is a cover for something far more sinister, the argument goes. “Even the Bible says the devil comes as an angel of light,” Pastor Norton told me. “Just because somebody’s sweet doesn’t mean they’re right.”

It doesn’t help the Democrat that, like many in the party, he dabbled in the kind of heady progressive rhetoric trendy in the early 2020s, something anathema to red-state voters. Among the hits, of which Texans are regularly reminded in Paxton’s speeches, Trump’s posts, and endless campaign ads: Talarico’s remark in 2021 that “God is nonbinary”; his comment in the same year that there are “six really common biological sexes” and his description of himself as “a Christian who hates Christianity”; his 2022 run for reelection to the Texas House, which he said would be a vegan campaign, reasoning that reducing meat consumption was “necessary to fight climate change”; and his comment that the American flag is a “complicated symbol.”

Talarico has since walked back some of these lines, calling them “cringey” and “provocative.” But Musk’s money cannon ensures Texas voters are relentlessly confronted by them, and the race appears to have tightened in the final stretch of the campaign. For voters susceptible to these kinds of criticisms of Talarico, a Paxton rally provides a potent narrative. The notes from his stump speech that draw the loudest applause can drive the neutral observer to mild psychosis. We’re going to stop Sharia law from coming to Texas, goes one. The Pfizer vaccine was less than 1% effective, offers another. And of course: James Talarico wants to trans your kids.

Paxton was greeted by a sea of red hats as he arrived onstage.

That last bit is one of Paxton’s favorites, and it hit hard in some of the more incandescent-red counties we passed through. “I mean, this guy is really obsessed with transitions,” Paxton mused into the mic, winding up for the big delivery. “He wants to transition our kids, he wants to transition Texas off of the oil and gas industry.” (Wry pause.) “How about we transition him and his crazy ideas right out of Texas!” (Applause, cheers, hoots, and hollers as Paxton stepped back from the podium and smirked, almost bashfully, eyes darting back and forth as he soaked up the response.)

Some of the attacks on Talarico are more extreme. Paxton and a number of his campaign surrogates warned that the Democrat would help usher Sharia law into Texas. When I met with Bannon, he introduced me to Patriot Mobile cofounder Glenn Story, who’s active in Texas politics and counts Paxton as a friend. “I’m the one who told him to start talking about Sharia law,” Story said. “You go up to the Costco near me? Towelheads everywhere,” he said, using a slur for Muslims. “Come with me, I’ll show you.” Reluctant to spend my afternoon driving around looking for people who might appear Muslim, I declined.

At a stop in Sanger, a small town in a ruby-red county north of Dallas, the star of the warm-up acts was Brandon Gill, a young House Republican who has emerged as a favorite among the party’s hard-line base. He walked out to a roaring welcome, and one man shouted, “Brandon for president!” The heckle was deftly parried by Gill: “Let’s say Ken Paxton for Senate first.” As Gill ran through the list of well-worn criticisms of Talarico’s liberalism, Stacey, a woman in the crowd, shouted: “It’s demonic!”

“That’s right,” Gill replied. “It is demonic.”

Outside the venue, I spoke with Stacey and her friend Claire, two Paxton superfans from nearby who called themselves “MAHA moms.”

“He seems like a nice man,” Stacey said of Talarico. “He’s just misguided. If he was my neighbor, I’d vote for him to be on my HOA board. But not for the Senate.” They were confident that Paxton would keep the seat red. But Claire was concerned that her parents, both Republicans, had written in names in protest of Paxton’s candidacy.

On a good day, Ken Paxton is not a gifted orator. This was a bad day. It was Sunday night, the last stop of the weekend, and the candidate walked onto a stage at Schulman’s Movie Bowl Grille in Sherman, a highway town 60 miles north of Dallas, to speak to a few dozen supporters picking at tacos while leaning back in big pleather recliners.

By this point I had seen Paxton deliver his stump speech, a 15-minute case for his Senate candidacy, some half a dozen times. At Schulman’s Movie Bowl Grille, his delivery was pained. He seemed tired. He stumbled over his jokes, stopping and returning to the top after realizing he forgot the punch line. He struggled through a section meant to serve as a blistering indictment of his opponent, and he eventually spent several minutes looking down at the podium and listing Talarico’s crimes against Texas off a piece of paper as the crowd sat in silence.

At one point an elderly man with a walker had had enough.

“More enthusiasm!” he shouted from the audience.

Paxton looked up from his papers and out into the crowd. “What?”

“More enthusiasm!” the man shouted again.

“Yes,” Paxton said meekly. “We all need a little more enthusiasm to go to the polls.”

Trump never hesitates to remind voters at his rallies that Paxton “may not dress right, he may not talk perfectly, and he may not be the best-looking guy I’ve ever seen.” The candidate has a lazy eye, a casualty of a childhood accident in which a berry was thrown at his face, requiring multiple surgeries, and a subsequent college basketball injury. He presents as meek, almost sheepish, and speaks in a monotone that belies his reputation as a bare-knuckle radical. He slurs his words and stumbles over his lines.

Trump rallied the faithful for Paxton in Corpus Christi.

“Darrell,” he said at one stop, addressing Issa, “California arreddy has tt—you already have two senators, you d—we don’t need a third.” He’s less the guy you want to get a beer with, per the old campaign cliché, and more the guy you feel a bit sorry for when it’s his turn to address the room at a regional sales conference. At a Trump rally for Paxton in Lubbock, the president told the crowd that his praise of Jon Husted’s “very powerful ass” boosted the senator’s election campaign in Ohio. “Maybe I should do that with Ken Paxton,” he mused, “but I’m not sure your body is going to qualify.”

For Talarico and the Texas Democrats, who haven’t won a seat in the United States Senate since 1988, the Paxton campaign presents an extraordinary opportunity. “Billy Begala says: For the last 30 years, all you had to do to win in Texas is win the Republican primary and then go on vacation,” said veteran Democratic strategist Paul Begala, whose son Billy works in Texas politics. Paxton may have taken that truism a little too far. After announcing his candidacy for the Republican nomination in an appearance on Sean Hannity’s Fox News show, he “cleared his calendar and booked a hotel in Augusta, Georgia, during the storied Masters golf tournament,” according to the Associated Press, “a trip that cost Texas taxpayers at least $25,000.” Over July Fourth weekend, while Talarico hit the trail, Paxton was in Europe, sightseeing in London and Iceland with his rumored mistress. As Talarico raised tens of millions of dollars from small-dollar donations throughout the summer, Paxton struggled to keep up. A week before the general election, Talarico had raised $158 million to Paxton’s $39 million.

“Ken is a different type of candidate in modern times,” Bannon said. “He has a hardcore grassroots base, but he’s not a good fundraiser.” In the primary against Cornyn, Paxton “didn’t raise any serious money. This was primarily a grassroots-driven thing.”

Paxton, Bannon added, is “a populist fire-breather who is not particularly charismatic.”

The last-ditch operation to save the populist fire-breather who is not particularly charismatic came this week in the form of two Trump rallies. They may end up as the last major events of the campaign. On Thursday, the Paxton campaign announced it was canceling a rally in El Paso scheduled for Sunday, just two days before the election.

At the first of Trump’s appearances, in Corpus Christi, I watched from the press pen as Border Patrol union chief Paul Perez revved up the crowd with a question. “Is Texas Trump country?” he bellowed. A sea of bright red hats, bobbing in chaotic unison in a portside hangar, went ballistic. They had braved the rain and the dour mood spreading across the country to see a president in whom they very much still believed. But across Texas, the cracks in Trump’s support are deepening. Just two years after he beat Kamala Harris in the state by more than 1.5 million votes, The Economist’s poll tracker finds Trump’s approval in Texas is underwater by 18 points. This has fueled fears among the state’s Republicans that many of those who broke for Trump in 2024 could stay home this year or, God forbid, vote for the Democrat who thinks God is nonbinary.

Many rallygoers were decked out in full American flag regalia.

Another’s shirt echoed the Paxton campaign bus.

“Clearly, it has been a challenge for Ken to run during difficult personal times, but one of the reasons we admire him is that he is resilient,” said Matt Schlapp, the chairman of the Conservative Political Action Conference, who held a fundraiser for Paxton at his Virginia home last month. “He will win this race, but, like last time, there will be some fear and trembling along the way.”

Others in the coalition aren’t so sure. “Paxton is in deep shit,” Rich Baris, a pro-Trump pollster, said in a podcast appearance this week.

Trump may rally the base, but it’s hard to see how a historically unpopular president making the race about him helps with the broader electorate. After the president commanded Republicans to host a “Trumpapalooza” midterm convention that served more as a celebration of his presidency than as a typical party congress, Paxton privately told donors the event hurt his campaign. “When we did that convention—it dropped our numbers,” Paxton said, according to audio of his comments obtained by The New York Times. “Everybody’s numbers dropped. Right now, yeah, not good.”

At the rally in Corpus Christi, Trump spoke for more than an hour. He extolled the glories of his presidency and made little mention of Paxton. After airing a supercut video of Talarico’s cringiest comments, Trump turned to the crowd. “The only man standing between Texas and this raging lunatic is a man named President Donald J. Trump, thank you!” he said. As the crowd went wild, Trump added: “And I need the help of Paxton.”

On the Come and Take It bus tour, Paxton was less a glimpse of Trumpism’s future than a showcase of what might be left behind when Trump is gone. The familiar accommodations were still required: overlook the scandals, forgive the personal failings, keep faith with the fighter standing between you and the forces of darkness. But there was none of the showmanship that made those demands easier to accept in Trump. The Paxton cocktail is the controversy without the charisma—and a test of whether a record of pure allegiance to Trump is enough for a Republican to win Texas. Defeat may well announce the bitter end of pure Trumpism, or at least prove that Trump alone is the movement. When he leaves the White House in 2029, what will remain of it?

Paxton is not known for his oratory—or his skills as a fundraiser.

I'm a hardcore reality TV fan, who regularly watches drama-filled shows like The Real Housewives, Survivor (which is streaming with a Paramount+ subscription) and The Traitors. For some lighter fare (pun intended) I decided to watch the new season of Great British Baking Show with my Netflix subscription, and I've found the series endlessly charming. I'm not one who typically gets hungry watching bakes, but Pastry Week had me drooling.

There's been a ton of discourse about the new season of Bake Off. Some fans are upset about the twists, while others can't get over judge Nigella Lawson's way of eating. Regarding the actual bakes of the show, I think that Pastry Week by far had the most mouthwatering choices. Let me explain.

I like the occasional sweet treat on special occasions, but I'm not necessarily a dessert person. Instead of ordering one after dinner I'd usually opt for another appetizer instead. Even when snacking at home I prefer savory treats like pretzels and popcorn over baked goods. Perhaps this means I'm not the choice demographic to watch Bake Off, but I'm largely watching the competition series for the low-stakes drama and British charm.

Aside from Bread Week (which was chock full of epic fails) most of the bakes this season have been sweet treats. That switched up during Pastry Week, with the remaining bakers making a number of savory treats that I wish I could have reached into the TV and tried. Seriously, why haven't they made the Wonkavision technology from Willy Wonka & the Chocolate Factory yet?

The Signature Challenge immediately had my stomach growling, so much so that I ordered Chinese Food to my house so I could properly enjoy the latest episode of The Great British Baking Show. Tom's Banh Mi pies looked incredible, as did Moyin's take on a Nigerian meat pie and Connie's jerk chicken pies.

While we went back into dessert land for Nigella's technical, the Showstopper Challenge once again brought savory goodness Bake Off. It was once again Connie, and Tom who created pies that I was dying to try. The latter ended up winning Star Baker for the third time as a result of his work, and it certainly seemed like he deserved it.

I traveled to Ireland and Northern Island last year, and I found myself obsessed with some of the savory baked goods during that time. Seriously, why aren't sausage rolls a thing in the United States? While I ponder this question I might just re-watch the latest episode of Bake Off. Although I won't be doing it on an empty stomach.

New episodes of The Great British Baking Show air Fridays on Netflix as part of the 2026 TV schedule. I assume the remaining episodes will mostly be about sweet treats, but who knows? Maybe the savory lovers like me will be treated to one or more of these bakes. Fingers crossed.

#3620. Everything You Should See Along With ‘You Can See Everything’

Jeff Somers is a freelancer who has been writing about writing, books, personal finance, and home maintenance since 2012.

Jeff has published nine novels and more than 70 short stories; his story Ringing the Changes was selected for inclusion in The Best American Mystery Stories 2006. In 2018, Jeff published the book Writing Without Rules: How to Write & Sell a Novel Without Guidelines, Experts, or (Occasionally) Pants. He holds a bachelor’s degree in English and previously worked in medical publishing as a production editor.

When not writing, Jeff spends his free time fixing up his old house. He has tackled a wide range of DIY projects, including remodeling a bathroom entirely on his own in two weeks, and building a roof deck that hasn't fallen down yet. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

You Can See Everything, the new documentary about Theranos founder (and accomplished con artist) Elizabeth Holmes from filmmakers Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim, is breaking records (and brains). Not only is it raking it in at the box office in a way that few documentaries can manage, it’s also dominating the pop culture chat right now thanks to genre-defying techniques; a huge, rule-breaking twist (that I won't spoil); and its unrepentant and inexplicably mesmerizing subject.

While some might argue that you should head into this incredible film experience fresh, if you’re unfamiliar with any of the three major figures involved, you will benefit from a little prep work before you head in—and if you've already seen it, you're no doubt eager to dive even deeper into this truly remarkable (in every sense of the word) story. Here’s what you should watch, read, and listen to before or after You Can See Everything.

To put it simply: There’s a lot going on here. To ensure you can appreciate the film, you should make sure you know at least the basics about three things: Elizabeth Holmes (and why she’s infamous), and the work of both Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. Here’s the crash course.

The 2019 podcast The Dropout is one of the most efficient ways to get the background on Holmes and Theranos. In the style of a true crime podcast, this show from ABC and journalist Rebecca Jarvis offers a deep dive into Holmes and her crimes that will give you all the background you’ll need.

John Carreyrou is the journalist who broke the Holmes story wide open, and his award-winning book Bad Blood offers a more journalistic and less sensational investigation than other accounts, providing a close-up look at Holmes in her CEO persona—an alternately terrifying and charismatic person who comes across as a “character” Holmes is playing. The book will inform your viewing of the documentary in important ways.

While Nathan Fielder is getting most of the attention for You Can See Everything, co-director Lance Oppenheim brings his signature technique to the film—it wouldn’t be nearly as interesting without his visual sensibility and framing.

Oppenheim has helmed several notable films, as he’s made a name for himself as a brilliant documentarian over the last few years, but to get ready for You Can See Everything, check out Spermworld, his 2024 exploration of unregulated sperm donations (you read that right). The doc deals with people who are as reality-challenged, manipulative, and possibly delusional as Holmes, and it will prep you for his visual style of extreme close-ups and excessive coverage that seems almost impossible in a normal documentary setting. You can stream Spermworld on Hulu.

If you’re unfamiliar with Nathan Fielder’s work, you need to strap in, because he’s unlike any other comedian or documentarian you’ve ever encountered.

To get a sense of his style, start with Nathan for You, a comedy-documentary-reality TV hybrid in which Fielder—as a version of himself—tries to use his business experience to help struggling people and small businesses. Presented as totally sincere, Fielder’s ideas are nevertheless increasingly elaborate and, in a word, unhinged. This show will familiarize you with Fielder’s persona and approach, but if you only have time to cram one episode, check out the series finale, “Finding Frances.” It follows Fielder’s attempts to reunite one of his earlier clients with his long-lost love, and it is a nearly perfect encapsulation of his style and approach. You can stream Nathan for You on HBO Max, Hoopla or Paramount Plus, or rent it episode-by-episode on Prime Video.

You should also watch at least some of Fielder’s other series, The Rehearsal. Here, Fielder (again, portraying a version of himself) attempts to help people prepare for difficult conversations utilizing increasingly outlandish techniques and scenarios that spiral into comedic insanity, including building sets, hiring actors, and immersing himself and his subjects in an alternate reality of sorts—an approach that will prepare you for some of You Can See Everything’s swerves. If you don’t have time to watch the whole thing, just check out the first episode, “Orange Juice, No Pulp.” It’s a self-contained chapter and will give you the basics. You can stream The Rehearsal on Apple TV or HBO Max, or rent episodes on Prime Video.

Have more bandwidth before watching You Can See Everything, or want a deeper dive after the documentary has melted your brain? Here’s what else you can check out.

The companion podcast to Carreyrou’s book, Bad Blood: The Final Chapter, is well worth a listen. Hearing the journalist’s perspective about his investigation and work during and after Holmes’ trial offers additional insight into her personality and methods that will really resonate after watching her in Fielder and Oppenheim’s doc.

Once you’ve noodled on You Can See Everything for a moment, there are two more movies you should check out.

For more on Holmes’s specific grift and how she pulled it off, Alex Gibney’s excellent The Inventor: Out for Blood in Silicon Valley is the way to go, especially if you didn’t follow the Theranos story closely at the time and your main visual guide to Holmes is the new documentary. Gibney’s film is more traditional, but offers a wealth of insight into Holmes and her bubble. You can stream The Inventor on HBO Max or rent it on Prime VIdeo.

If you more from co-director Lance Oppenheim, watch Some Kind of Heaven, his 2020 breakout documentary about The Villages retirement community in Florida. It’s the film that put Oppenheim on the map, and offers hints of the same detached observational style that makes You Can See Everything so arresting. You can stream Some Kind of Heaven on Kanopy or Hoopla, or rent it on Prime Video.

Speaking of which, if you loved the visual style and “enhanced” reality of You Can See Everything and want to see more of that, catch the Robert Pattinson-starring Primetime, still in theaters. It’s Oppenheim's narrative film directorial debut, and combines his hyperstyled visual flair with thriller pacing and a narrative based on a true story.

The Curse, Fielder’s 2023 TV series, is his first work of fiction, and it offers some fascinating insights. It follows a newly married couple (played by Fielder and Emma Stone) who struggle to get an HGTV-style show off the ground as things get excruciatingly awkward (and, eventually, kind of surreal). After watching You Can See Everything, it will be interesting to see how Fielder views the power of editing, the ethics of reality TV, and working with a name actor to get the results that he wants. Plus, similarly to the film, The Curse swerves into a final act that will melt your brain. You can stream The Curse on Apple TV or rent it on Prime Video.

You should also definitely watch The Dropout, the 2022 Hulu series starring Amanda Seyfried. It’s a well-made film, and Seyfried’s performance was rightly praised for capturing the weirdness of Holmes' public persona. You can stream The Dropout on Hulu.

#3619. GOG Wants To Bring Back Physical PC Games, But There’s A Catch

While PlayStation 5 console owners are preparing for a discless future, PC gamers have been living in all-digital world for decades now. The advent of Steam and cheaper broadband internet helped end physical PC game sales in the early 2000s, but GOG is dreaming up a future where these games can thrive once again--if it can get past a few obstacles that stand in its way.

Speaking to GamesRadar, Marcin Paczynski, GOG's senior business development and partnerships manager, laid out a dream scenario in which a consumer can browse GOG, select a game, and have a physical copy delivered to their home. "Ideally, my dream would be to be able to buy physical versions of those games on GOG," Paczynski said. "You go to your shelf on GOG, you click on the game that you would like to receive a physical copy of, you order it, and it gets to you. That would be a perfect scenario."

While that sounds ideal, it's easier said than done, as Paczynski noted that selling physical goods is a logistical challenge when compared to running a digital storefront. Physical media requires organizing storage, delivery, and additional publisher approvals, but Paczynski hopes to see it realized one day.

It's worth noting that the GOG Preservation Program did recently create high-resolution scans for five classic games--Myst, Descent, Hitman: Codename 47, Star Trek: 25th Anniversary, and Armikrog--and turned them into 3D models that you can view on your PC--as well as printable files for anyone looking for a papercraft project. It's similar to the work done by another site, Big Box Collection, which offers a far larger library of classic PC boxes to admire in 3D.

GOG isn't the only company nostalgic for the big boxes of a bygone era; several sites have popped up in recent years to offer curated collections of physical PC and console games. From Limited Run Games to Special Reserve Games, there's still an appetite for owning something with a tangible quality.

#3618. Which 'FBI' Stars Are — And Aren't — Returning After Onscreen Death, Firing?

FBI is returning for season 9 — but is everyone from the cast coming back?

Created by Law & Order creator Dick Wolf, FBI, which premiered in 2018, follows the agents of the Federal Bureau of Investigation in New York City. The personnel have endured their fair share of ups and downs — with Maggie (Missy Peregrym) going through a tragedy when serial slasher Ray DiStefano (Matthew Rauch) kidnapped and killed her sister, Erin (Adrienne Rose Bengtsson).

“I think it’s really important what we’re doing, because we’re highlighting how to move forward. Everybody experiences loss. Everybody goes through the depths of emotions in life,” she explained to Deadline in March. “You have an opportunity to show connection, relationship, intimacy and growth. And this is exactly why I do what I do. I hope this makes people feel seen and that they want to keep going after such a horrific experience, and that they don’t give up.”

Peregrym was hopeful about the plans for the show.

“To go so far. I was like, ‘What are we doing after this?’ You know, I’ve been playing the same character for eight years, and we’re going so far,” she noted. “What’s the plan? How are we going to move through the next steps of getting back on your feet and being able to be in the world again? We’re not a drama where we sit around in our underwear and chat on the couch. We’ve got to get back to work.”

She concluded, “So at what point are we going to address the reality of this scenario, and we are, we are doing it in the best way that we can with our show, like the way we do it on a procedural. But you know, as much as it scared me, I was terrified to go into that space at the end. I’m finding it really interesting to play my character now and finding these beats of when I can insert this stuff and when to work. And it’s just a challenge. It just feels like we’re doing a new show again. Do you know what I mean? And maybe that’s a gift.”

Keep scrolling to see who else is and isn’t returning to FBI for season 9:

Peregrym recently denied plans to leave the show after Maggie mourned the loss of her sister.

“I’ll be honest. I’m on a procedural show, and I wonder what impact this is possibly making? And sometimes I get freaked out because I think we’re just highlighting some of the horrors of humanity every week,” Peregrym told Deadline in March. “And what is this? What are we doing this for? What am I investing a lot of my life in to do this for?”

Zaki’s OA isn’t going anywhere — but his story line will look a little different in season 9 after going undercover.

Jubal a.k.a Sisto’s fan-favorite character is once again front and center when the show returns.

De la Garza is expected to come back as Isobel after originally joining the show as a guest star in season 1.

It is very likely that if Boyd’s Scola left FBI then the fans would riot — so there isn’t any concern that he won’t return.

After joining the show in season 8, Martinez expressed her hope that she would remain on the show as Eva Ramos.

“Before I came into the show, I sat down with showrunner Mike Weiss and told me who he was thinking Eva was going to be. That was really the deciding factor for me to be like, ‘Yes, this is something that’s very interesting to me. This is something that I think I can offer and give value to and make it exciting and different,'” she exclusively told Us Weekly. “When you join a new show, you get the opportunity to do something different. It was definitely like, ‘OK, how can you show different sides of a profession? How can you show how different women approach something differently?'”

VanSanten is officially back as Nina later in the season.

#3617. Borderlands Franchise Hits 100 Million Sales As Gearbox Hints At What’s Next

The Borderlands franchise has reached a new sales milestone, as developer Gearbox Software announced that Borderlands 4 had pushed the series over the 100 million units sold mark. Celebrating the achievement, the studio also took time to reveal what's next for Borderlands 4 as it enters its second year, as well as plans it's busy cooking up for the IP.

"We just wrapped our Year 1 roadmap, and the team is cooking hard on more Borderlands 4 content for next year," Gearbox wrote in a blog post, adding that weekly activity refreshes and Community Challenges will continue in the game. So what's next for Borderlands? Gearbox says that it's "a bigger look at the franchise as a whole," and it's also listening to fans to gauge which characters they want to spend more time with.

Don't expect Gearbox to drop a Borderlands 5 announcement anytime soon, as the developer said it needs time and space to work on future projects. "Big plans take time, and we need some room to work. You can trust that we’ll talk more when the time is right," Gearbox added. Thirteen months ago, Gearbox Software boss Randy Pitchford had predicted that Borderlands 4 would continue to sell millions of copies and would help the franchise cross the 100 million units sold line eventually. "We will break 100 million units with this launch, easily, all in, with the franchise," Pitchford said at the time.

To put that in perspective, the Borderlands franchise had sold 94 million units through August 2025, meaning Borderlands 4 would move at least 6 million copies. Historically, Borderlands 2 is the franchise's top seller, with 31 million units sold, while Borderlands 3 is second with 23 million sales to date. It's worth noting that these games have also gone on sale regularly--with Borderlands 3 once being sold for just $3 on PC via Steam--and Borderlands 4 has also received a few discounts since launch. Gearbox and publisher Take-Two Interactive haven't revealed sales figures for Borderlands 4 yet, so it's hard to know where it currently fits on the Borderlands sales chart.

The game didn't have a smooth launch either, as various technical hurdles required multiple rounds of patching, and the oft-delayed Switch 2 edition was eventually paused so that Gearbox could focus on the PC, PS5, and Xbox Series X|S editions of the game.

#3616. The Mamdanis Take Manhattan!

Billionaire Michael Bloomberg attended plenty of museum galas when he was mayor of New York City. Bill de Blasio didn’t—not even the Brooklyn Artists Ball at the Brooklyn Museum, a quick 30-minute walk up Prospect Park West from his beloved neighborhood of Park Slope. Eric Adams couldn’t wait to get his own tickets to art shindigs; in 2022, a few months into his one-and-only term as mayor, he arrived at the Met Gala red carpet wearing a long leather jacket emblazoned with the words “End Gun Violence.”

“I walk around with swagger in my pocket,” Adams told ABC News from the red carpet.

The city’s current head of government, Zohran Mamdani, is perhaps the most culturally literate mayor since Ed Koch. Or maybe ever—he instructed the city to invest over $320 million in the Department of Cultural Affairs, the largest amount in New York history. And he pays attention to the smaller sums too. When the department announced that city-funded grants for artists would double from $5,000 to $10,000, Mamdani filmed a video of himself, brush in hand, behind an easel, trying his best to paint dollar signs à la Warhol.

“Not everyone’s an artist!” he says, flashing that Mamdani grin. “But a lot of New Yorkers are.”

But when would he show up in a tux to one of the primo arts institution fundraisers that dot the social calendar, particularly as the fall season starts humming?

And now he has. Mamdani has officially attended his first art gala as mayor: the Studio Museum Gala, held at The Glasshouse this past Monday evening. Celebrating the museum’s first year in its new building, it raised over $4 million for the institution. While mingling among guests at the cocktail hour, Mamdani, who did indeed put on a tux for the occasion, posed for photos with First Lady Rama Duwaji and luminaries, such as collector Bernard Lumpkin and the artist Rashid Johnson.

The event was honoring longtime board chair Ray McGuire, the Lazard president and mega art collector who’s served as chair of the Studio Museum’s board for 23 years—and, in case you forgot, ran his own quixotic campaign for mayor in 2021. Through all the toasts, Mayor Mamdani and the first lady sat next to Studio Museum director Thelma Golden.

Mamdani has a bit of a history with the Studio Museum—it’s where he spent his most recent birthday, checking out work by Taylor Simmons, the Atlanta native currently in the museum’s residency program.

Rama Duwaji, Thelma Golden, Zohran Mamdani, Kathryn Chenault, Rashid Johnson, and Lake Bell

As it turns out, the world’s most famous mayor has had a hell of a week museum-going. On Monday, he also released a video filmed at The Met—it featured Mamdani standing in the Rockefeller Wing and wandering through the Great Hall. In it, he informs us that The Met is not just a place to check out pre-Columbian masterworks: It’s also a place to cast your vote.

“Only in New York City can you vote in places like the Metropolitan Museum of Art,” he says.

The Met and the Studio Museum are both part of the Cultural Institutions Group, a subset of New York cultural mainstays that receive funding from the city. Other institutions on that list include El Museo Del Barrio, the Brooklyn Museum and the Bronx Museum of the Arts. Cherished institutions such as, say, the Whitney Museum of American Art don’t receive city money, though that hasn’t stopped Mamdani from extending his support to them. A few weeks into his mayoralty, he alighted to the Whitney’s Renzo Piano–designed building in the Meatpacking District to announce a few mayoral appointments and a ban on junk fees on hotel bookings. He also gave the museum’s programming a shout-out.

“One of the last times I was here I saw the wonderful exhibition of Alvin Ailey,” he said, referring to “Edges of Ailey,” which was up at the Whitney in late 2024.

Later in the year, Duwaji stopped by one of the museum’s fundraisers, the Whitney Art Party—though the mayor did not attend with her. That evening, January 27, Mamdani instead made a surprise appearance on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon.

I’ve been tracking Mamdani’s interest in New York’s gallery scene since at least February 2025, when I was invited to a “Party for Zohran” at the Avenue A music venue Night Club 101. The event was co-hosted by Tribeca gallery Theta and Greene Naftali’s Carol Greene, as well as artists such as Martine Syms, Ser Serpas, and Aria Dean. “The art world is coalescing around a mayoral candidate,” the publicist Kaitlin Phillips, who was brought in to do PR for Mamdani early in his primary campaign, texted me in mid-February 2025, back when his campaign still seemed like a major long shot.

On March 2, I went to the party. After taking in some performances and live podcasts, Mamdani and I stepped outside to chat on Avenue A, talking about the art scene, which he was still getting fully acquainted with. He did, however, understand what it’s like to be an artistically minded person in New York.

“I think for me... Look, I’m the son of a filmmaker. I’m a failed artist myself,” he told me, though I still think the track kinda bangs. “I think that ultimately politics and art, there’s a commonality in the act of storytelling.”

I asked him about his platform for the arts in New York City.

Read True Colors: Inside the global deals and colorful critiques that make the art world go round, with a weekly guide to the must-see openings, auctions, and fairs.

“At the core is a belief that art is something that every New Yorker deserves in their life,” Mamdani said back then. “And that that is not something that can simply be restricted to the museums or a Museum Mile, but it is something that also is committed to the community organizations and neighborhoods in the outer boroughs that are, for many New Yorkers, the only conduit to having that.”

Since taking office, Mamdani has named Diya Vij, an arts-organizations veteran, to lead the Department of Cultural Affairs, and assembled a slew of heavyweights to serve on his Committee on Arts and Culture. He’s also started picking board members for various museums. His campaign deputy Elana Leopold sits on the MoMA board, while Battery Park City CEO Raju Mann sits on the board of MoMA PS1.

As far as we know, though, no word has surfaced on who will be the mayor’s rep on The Met board—the most powerful perch of them all. Adams picked Scott Sartiano as his rep early in his term, and his fellow board members have indicated to me that Sartiano was an active board member who was pivotal and energizing for the team. (I wrote a whole profile on Sartiano, pegged to the rise of Zero Bond, back in 2024.)

But I’m sure it’ll be a thoughtful pick. Even through his meteoric rise, the mayor’s platform for artists in New York hasn’t really changed since that night we chatted on Avenue A.

“Artists have brought imagination and honesty to every corner of our city—from our sidewalks and subways to our museums, parks, and theaters. For generations, they have come to New York to explore, create, and challenge convention, shaping our city’s identity and drawing people from around the world,” Mayor Mamdani told me in a statement. “My administration is committed to supporting them and ensuring every New Yorker can experience the arts. We doubled city-funded grants for artists for the first time in nearly 20 years, and we’re partnering with organizations like TDF, The Met, and cultural institutions across the city to expand access to free and low-cost Broadway and opera tickets, as well as free admission to more than 20 cultural institutions. Because the arts are essential to who we are as a city, and every New Yorker should have the opportunity to experience them.”

Johnny Depp is an accomplished character actor with a long and wildly successful career. Arguably one of Depp's best roles is as Captain Jack Sparrow in the Pirates of the Caribbean movies, which are streaming in their entirety with a Disney+ subscription. I didn't expect the 63 year-old to have jokes when talking about possibly returning to the franchise alongside Orlando Bloom's Will Turner.

While Depp will return to theaters in Ebenezer this month, some moviegoers are hoping to see him return in a future Pirates of the Caribbean movie. During a recent interview with People, the Edward Scissorhands actor was asked about possibly returning to the beloved franchise, and responded with:

Well, I think we should have a contest of who can grow the fastest non-beard. Because neither of us can grow a beard, I don’t think. I can’t, for sure, but maybe he can. I don’t know.

Shots fired. Despite having facial hair in the Pirates of the Caribbean films, it turns out that neither Johnny Depp nor Orlando Bloom can actually grow a beard. While sidestepping whether or not he'd be down to return as Jack Sparrow, the Sweeney Todd actor was sure to poke fun at both himself, and his famous co-star.

Ebenezer marks Depp's first real return to a big Hollywood movie since the verdict of his defamation trial with Amber Heard was revealed. He spent a few years living abroad and getting out of the spotlight, but he's back playing the title role of Ti West's forthcoming holiday movie. Only time will tell if the upcoming book to screen adaptation ends up being considered one of the best Christmas movies of all time, but it seems like a game changer for the actor.

There's been chatter about more Pirates movies for a few years. At one point multiple movies were in development, including one that would star Margot Robbie. Unfortunately, there hasn't been any concrete updates about one of these projects moving forward in the development process. Although with Johnny Depp returning to the big screen, I have to assume that the chatter surrounding the franchise, and his possible return as Captain Jack Sparrow, will get louder.

Depp starred as the protagonist in all five of the Pirates of the Caribbean movies, which ran in theaters from 2003 to 2017. The same can't be said for Orlando Bloom, who was absent for On Stranger Tides. He ended up returning in Dead Men Tell No Tales, which is the most recent installment in the action/adventure property.

All five of the Pirates of the Caribbean movies are streaming now on Disney+. Only time will tell if a sixth movie ends up being green lit by the powers that be at Disney, but there does seem to be a ton of chatter about that possibility online.

#3614. The Best Apple Watch for Most People Is Over $100 Off

The Apple Watch Series 10 was released in September 2024, and it's one of the best ways to get into the Apple Watch in 2026 without breaking the bank. Right now, the titanium 46 mm case model with cellular capabilities is $112 off, bringing the price down to $637 (originally $749). That's the lowest price after Apple raised prices this summer due to the RAM shortage, according to price-tracking tools. The same model in gold titanium is also over $100 off, reaching $679 (originally $799), saving you the same amount compared to the latest Series 12 going for $799.

The Apple Watch Series 10 was considered the best Apple Watch for most people last fall and is a great replacement if you're still wearing the more budget SE. There are also some key upgrades from the Apple Watch 9, although they're less noticeable than previous Apple Watch upgrades. If you're curious to know how it compares to other flagship smartwatches from its time, you can check out our head-to-head comparison.

Some of the first things you'll notice on the Series 10 are a thin case and a big OLED screen (either 1.6 inches or 1.8 inches, depending on which model you get). The Series 10 has audio playback, meaning you can listen to podcasts, take calls, or listen to Spotify on its speakers. The sleep features allow notifications for signs of sleep apnea. What you're giving up by saving on this version over the latest Series 12 is a faster S11 chip, a newer Health Sensing System and the Readiness app (tracks daily insights, vitals, and other metrics), a longer battery life (from 18 to 24 hours), 5G RedCap support (it helps save on battery life and has better network coverage compared to 5G), and audio intelligence features like Live Rewind, Siri Recap, and Sound Recognition.

If those extra features don't matter to you, the Series 10 is a great Apple Watch to get in 2026 at a discount, when many are still suffering from their price hikes.

#3613. Justin Timberlake Releasing 4-Part ‘Tell-All’ Docuseries With Janet Jackson

Justin Timberlake is reportedly working on a “tell-all” docuseries that will explore his Super Bowl scandal with Janet Jackson and his relationship with ex Britney Spears.

The “Selfish” singer, 45, is partnering with Apple on a four-part project directed by Fisher Stevens, who has previously made documentaries about Hollywood legend Carrie Fisher and soccer great David Beckham, per Variety.

The docuseries will reportedly feature an interview with Jackson, 60, about her and Timberlake’s infamous Super Bowl XXXVIII Halftime Show appearance, in which one of Jackson’s breasts was exposed on live TV due to a wardrobe malfunction.

Little else about the project is known, as of publication, though the series is expected to premiere on Apple TV+ in December.

Us has reached out to Timberlake and Jackson’s representatives for comment.

The 2004 Super Halftime Show at Houston’s Reliant Stadium sparked a national controversy — along with igniting conspiracy theories about whether the wardrobe malfunction was a public stunt. The shocking finale of the performance featured Timberlake ripping away part of Jackson’s costume, exposing her mostly uncovered right breast.

The subsequent national debate about “indecency” led directly to increased censorship on radio. The United States House of Representatives later voted to increase maximum FCC fines from $32,500 to $325,000 per violation as part of the Broadcast Decency Enforcement Act.

Timberlake has always maintained that the wardrobe malfunction was entirely accidental. He told Apple Music’s Beats 1 host Zane Lowe in 2018 that he’d “absolutely” made peace with Jackson in the years since the controversy.

“I don’t know that a lot of people know that,” he added. “I don’t think it’s my job to do that because you value the relationships that you do have with people.”

The “Rhythm Nation” singer echoed Timberlake’s sentiments in her own 2022 Lifetime documentary Janet Jackson, in which she insisted the Super Bowl scandal was “blown way out of proportion.”

“It was an accident that should not have happened, but everyone is looking for someone to blame and that’s gotta stop,” she stressed. “Justin and I are very good friends and we will always be very good friends.”

Meanwhile, Spears, 44, wrote extensively about her three-year relationship with Timberlake in her 2023 memoir The Woman in Me, including sharing a bombshell revelation that she cheated on him with choreographer Wade Robson. The “Toxic” singer also accused Timberlake of infidelity during their relationship.

Spears later publicly apologized for “some of the things [she] wrote” in her autobiography and may have offered Timberlake an olive branch.

“If I offended any of the people I genuinely care about I am deeply sorry,” she wrote via Instagram in January 2024. ”

She added, “I wanted to say I am in love with Justin Timberlake’s new song ‘Selfish.’”

Timberlake did not directly address The Woman in Me, though he told a New York City concert crowd in January 2024 that he was going to “apologize to absolutely f***ing nobody.”

No title for Timberlake’s Apple docuseries has been announced as of publication.

#3612. Drake’s Stylist Juliet Charlotte Has Seen All Your Memes

Stylist Sessions is a series of conversations in which Vanity Fair’s style correspondent, José Criales-Unzueta, unpacks the details, strategies, and Easter eggs on red carpets with the leading stylists. Up next, Juliet Charlotte tells VF about dressing Drake and, yes, reading all your comments about his looks

If you have access to the internet, it’s likely that you’ve seen what Drake wore to celebrate his 40th birthday last weekend in New York City. The rapper opted for a pair of red Versace leather pants and a cheetah jacket, a customized Chrome Hearts jeans and a suede vest, and an archival Chanel scarf paired with gray sweats. But it was an Hermès by Martin Margiela fringed shawl from 1997—a bonafide fashion vintage holy grail—that launched a thousand memes. Drake stepped out, and the jokes poured in: he was dubbed “pumpkin spice papi,” a nod to his nickname and Instagram handle @champagnepapi, described as a Real Housewife on a girls trip to Aspen, and as someone ready for “Christian girl autumn,” another viral trend.

Drake has been the punchline in culture many times, but—online trolls be damned—he’s been dressing better than ever. Chalk that up to his new-ish stylist, New Jersey native Juliet Charlotte. The 27-year-old started her career working with Ye and his fashion brand, Yeezy, as part of his wider styling team. Now that she’s a year into working with Drake, she’s based in Toronto. She also styles the up-and-coming Canadian singer-songwriter Chxrry, whose debut album U, Me & My Ego was released earlier this year.

Charlotte is a singular kind of stylist, particularly in that she prefers to buy pieces—some new, most archival—to build archives for her clients instead of borrowing clothes that any other celebrity could wear. In her first-ever interview, she tells VF about dressing Drake, and addresses the many memes. Spoiler alert: She’s seen them and remains unfazed—she even found some of them funny.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity.

Vanity Fair: How did you get into styling?

Juliet Charlotte: I started styling five years ago now. I had just turned 21. Kanye’s team reached out to me, his GM [general manager] at the time, this guy named Laurence Chandler. They were like, “Are you a stylist? Can you come in and do some fittings with us?” I was literally a college student working a retail job, and I was like, Yes, I am a stylist. Of course I can [laughs]. It was around the time of the pandemic, when Ye was at the Mercedes-Benz Stadium and working with Demna. I walked into this room and there’s Demna and all these Balenciaga clothes and Ye. I just wanted to work. I was excited, and I just pretended that I knew what I was doing. I ended up working with him up until maybe two years ago now. I learned a lot from that experience, and then I took on new clients. I worked with [rapper and singer] Molly Santana, and now Chxrry and Drake.

Why do you think they thought you were a stylist?

I was going to school for fashion in New Jersey, and I didn’t actually know which area of fashion I wanted to enter. I just knew that I always loved clothes. When the pandemic happened, all the stores closed, so I had to find a new way to make money. I started to make angel number necklaces, and it just blew up and it was really profitable for me. Looking back, it’s kind of embarrassing, but I was young and it allowed me to buy clothes that I wanted. I would take pictures and post on my Instagram just casually. It wasn’t like I wanted to be an influencer or anything, I just wanted people to see the way I dress. It was a very casual thing, but Yeezy is very reference-based, and I guess I kept showing up on mood boards at that time. So Ye was like, let’s just get this girl in here.

I was part of a bigger team, and Ye would throw me into different roles. So it wasn’t always just styling. Sometimes I was working on e-commerce or doing campaigns, or sometimes it was Bianca [Censori]’s wardrobe. It’s really collaborative at Yeezy. There’s so many talented people that work on everything together.

I was wondering if there was a Ye or Yeezy connection, because I noticed an aesthetic throughline with your personal style. What would you say is your aesthetic, your “thing,” as a stylist?

The Yeezy background definitely helped make me this way, because I want to simplify everything and strip down everything and just be like, let’s just do the absolute best version of whatever you want to do. I’m always trying to declutter. And I really think that came from working with Ye, because he just wants to strip everything back and make it just simple but beautiful and effective.

Drake is a maximalist when it comes to his style, and I appreciate that. I don’t want to just throw my personal style on anybody that I work with. I really want to take what they love and be like, “Okay, let’s do the best version of this.” Working with him, I really just try and keep it in his world and keep it to things that excite him.

Drake out in New York City wearing vintage Hermès by Martin Margiela from 1997.

Hermès by Martin Margiela, fall-winter 1997.

Have you always been into vintage fashion? Or is it something that you’ve developed with Drake to build that into his wardrobe?

Obviously we just had that Hermès by [Martin] Margiela moment, which I really enjoyed and I thought it was fun. But I’m really interested in taking pieces, just random vintage pieces that didn’t get such a moment in the past, because that Hermès piece already had its moment on the runway. It’s fun to bring it back, but the way that I like to shop is finding vintage pieces that didn’t get a moment and reinventing them. Obviously there’s a lot of amazing designers right now, but I’m also not so into over-consumption, and just what we’ve turned into. I’d really rather shop vintage as much as I can.

Drake is someone who has such a wide range of influences and sounds. When you work on looks for him, are you trying to pull from this really wide range of inspirations and aesthetics, or are you trying to be a little more focused? Do you try to speak back to the music or do you just try to be a little more focused on just the look?

Sometimes we’re pulling inspiration from Michael Jackson or Liberace, or another artist. But, for example, we’re in Texas right now. He just bought a ranch in Texas. It’s so beautiful. When I first started working with him and I came to the ranch, I’m like, “You are a ranch owner. You’re not larping this aesthetic. You literally live it.” I was really inspired by the saddle shop that’s nearby and all these different stores because it’s two hours away from Houston. He was already wearing [Western clothing] when I met him. This is just a different variation of it. The Western stuff is heavily in his style now, loves vests. I take what I see in his everyday life and see what we lean on more. Like even this mob boss type of thing—he’s really interested in Italian culture, and I’m Italian, so that influence comes in as well.

He has had such a long and prolific career, and he is often self-referential. Do you ever reference early moments in his career?

We did just pull back in his “FOMO” video. We did a variation of the “Hotline Bling” outfit that he wore. But we really don’t draw back too much, I think because he’s just evolved so much as a person. I’ll still send him some looks and be like, “Oh, you ate this,” [laughs]. I have met him as the person that he is now and I’m like, “Okay, he just turned 40. Let’s just be elevated and grown.”

Chxrry at Paris Fashion Week in September.

Chxrry is building something really strong. What’s it like to work with both an artist that has been working in the industry for so long while also with someone who’s so green?

Chxrry and I have become best friends in the process, so we’re just figuring it out together. We’re the same age. She’s so early in her career that I’m sure she’ll have many evolutions, but for now it’s just about having fun.

With Drake, he just loves clothes and is pretty easygoing, but there’s obviously a lot more pressure that’s involved because he’s so established. It’s very different, but equally as rewarding.

I have to ask about the birthday outfits. I thought they were great, but I’m curious if you planned a birthday weekend wardrobe or if you are more casual about it?

Well, October’s a crazy month, so there’s so much stuff going on so I did a lot of preparation. We knew that we wanted to do a beautiful suit, but we actually had three other suits that fell through before that one. Last minute, our atelier had just made that tux for him, and then I got the brooch, we put on a bow tie. It all came together at the last minute, and that Chanel scarf I had just bought that morning in New York. The Hermès shawl I bought the day before we left for the trip in Canada. Everything is really just down to what he’s feeling like that night. We can do all this preparation, but that night if he’s like, “Actually, I just feel like being more chill or I just want to do this,” we just pivot, and we always figure it out.

Drake wearing gray sweats and a vintage Chanel scarf.

A Chorme Hearts cheetah jacket and Versace red leather pants.

I like that he seems to wear only things he owns, when many celebrities wear borrowed clothing. Do you also do that, or do you prefer to just buy things?

On the record [laughs], I hate pulling. I hate loaning. I hate all of that. It gives me anxiety. I hate if it was my stuff and it was out in the world and you just never know what happens. It could get messed up in travel, and there’s just wear and tear. Things just happen. I know it’s a huge part of styling, but for me, I’d rather just source the pieces myself and have them be a part of our archive and a part of our collection.

With someone like Drake, who is so big, you want there to be an archive of what he’s done and worn, otherwise it’s all lost in brands’ sample closets. I have to ask about the memes. People had so much to say about the Hermès by Margiela. As the stylist, what do you think of that?

I love a joke. I love a joke we can laugh about, but I still love the look. I don’t feel less than or like, “Oh God, it’s a meme.” I still love the look. I think it was amazing. Even when we did “FOMO” and he was wearing that leather jacket with the fur on one side, that was a women’s Saint Laurent piece. I love when men do things that are out of the box, or that isn’t just pants and a shirt. Why not wear a fringed shawl? I was into it, but I could appreciate the joke and I did think some of them were funny.

Pumpkin Spice Papi was really funny. If anything, becoming a meme nowadays adds to the look. It’s already a Halloween costume.

Yes [laughs], I’ve seen that. I was too young, but I always think that if we had the internet the way that we do now, what would people say about Michael Jackson or what would they say about Prince? I’m sure there would be so many memes. There would have to be.

Read Fit Check: Your front row seat to the power players, peacocks, and deep pockets of fashion—and how they influence the rest of the world.

You mentioned the Saint Laurent women’s jacket. Something that I always really liked about Drake’s style is his willingness to just go there and have fun with fashion. There’s something really cool and really refreshing about that.

It’s really just fun and it’s really just down to what we’re both happy with. And as a man, if you’re really comfortable with yourself and comfortable, and you know who you are... He gets so many opinions projected on him all the time and he just doesn’t care. He still chooses what he likes. It doesn’t change his mind. I think it’s just because he’s so confident and comfortable with who he is. It’s really refreshing to work with somebody who’s not like, “Oh no, I can’t wear that. That’s crazy,” or whatever. If anything, he’s just like, “Oh yeah, fuck it. Let’s do it.” He’s really just excited to try new things. And even the fringe shawl, we spoke about it afterwards and he was like, “Yeah, it was sick. I loved it.” There’s nothing that can change his mind.

People may not think I’m the best [stylist] or whatever, but I like it. I don’t trust anyone else’s opinion because you’re not in my shoes, so you can’t really tell me how I should do it. Drake as a person has so much fun with his life. He had a blast for his birthday weekend. He doesn’t care about comments and neither do I. We don’t sit there and read them. We’ll give a chuckle if it’s funny or share a meme, but keep it pushing. We have fun.

Joseph Zada may be the star tribute of Sunrise on the Reaping, but Mckenna Grace is absolutely the victor of the movie's press tour. Lately, she's been wearing a ton of amazing Hunger Games fashion, often inspired by Jennifer Lawrence, but I think she just stepped out in the best one yet on this Monday.

Grace went to the Berlin premiere of The Hunger Games prequel in an incredible reference to the best movie of the franchise. Check it out:

A post shared by visitBerlin (@visitberlin)

My jaw dropped when I saw this on Visit Berlin. Obviously, she's paying tribute to Jennifer Lawrence's fire-catching The Hunger Games: Catching Fire dress. Who can forget the moment when Katniss and Peeta turn up at the Tribute Parade in matching flaming outfits that takes the breath away of Panem? It's a key piece from the movie franchise, and I'm so happy Mckenna Grace decided to put her own spin on it.

I'll never forget the first time this dress came on screen in Catching Fire, and this tribute to it is just expertly executed. Bravo to Grace, and her team led by stylist Molly Dickson. She really is Mckenna's own Cinna.

I mean, it's moments like this what reminds me why I love celebrity fashion!This has to be a custom dress, right? It recaptures the dress from the movie SO WELL, from the halter top to the flames all over it. I especially love how the top of it is shimmery and how the bottom is completely red. It's as if the dress is completely engulfed in flames at its ends. Grace also wore a similar headpiece to the one J-Law's Katniss wears in the movie and had her hair styled in curls.

This is just one of many Hunger Games references Grace has been doing while promoting the 2026 movie release. Last month she also wore a dress very similar to Katniss's white gown and another one that referenced Rue's interview dress. Last week, she also turned up in an ensemble that looked just like the Hunger Games arena in her movie.

It's actually quite perfect for Grace to channel J-Law's Hunger Games fashion because in Sunrise on the Reaping, her character of Maysilee inspires Katniss. She's the first tribute in the games to wear the mockingjay pin. .

Sunrise on the Reaping takes place during the 25th Hunger Games when Haymitch Abernathy is chosen to compete at the age of 16. Since it's the first Quarter Quell, double the amount of tributes are chosen, which means there's four from each District chosen. It doesn't come out until November 20, but the first reactions came in last week, and the prequel is already being called "a near perfect Hunger Games movie".

As excited as I am, I'm also over here on the edge of my seat over what Grace do next as the movie's press tour continues!

#3609. Who Went Home on 'Dancing With the Stars' Disney Night? See Scores

Magic entered the Dancing With the Stars ballroom for season 35’s Disney Night — but one couple’s dreams didn’t come true.

With performances inspired by Disney stories and their Broadway adaptations, the remaining eight couples took the stage during the Monday, November 2, episode and wowed guest judge Cynthia Erivo.

“I just thought that was the most joyful thing ever to start this with,” Erivo, 39, told Amber Glenn and pro Pasha Pashkov after their quickstep to “A Star Is Born” from Hercules. “The strength that you both have is just glorious to watch. … Well done.”

After earning a perfect score during last week’s Horror Movie Night, Harry Shum Jr. and pro Jenna Johnson nailed their routine again — receiving another whopping 40 out of 40 from Erivo and judges Carrie Ann Inaba, Bruno Tonioli and Derek Hough.

“Honestly, the thing that I am really focused on is dance to express not to impress,” Shum said. “If people are impressed by what we express, then come on. Thank you. That’s my north star.”

While Jenna Dewan and pro Val Chmerkovskiy received the second perfect score of the night, Shum and Johnson were granted immunity from next week’s dance off due to having a higher combined score throughout the season.

Team dances also made a return to the ballroom, as cohost Alfonso Ribeiro competed with captain Tatyana Ali and pro Jan Ravnik, Maura Higgins and pro Mark Ballas, Julia Stiles and Ezra Sosa, and Glenn and Pashkov for a routine to Zootopia 2’s “Zoo.” They earned a 36 out of 40.

Cohost Julianne Hough then laced up her dancing shoes for High School Musical’s “We’re All In This Together” with captain Connor Wood and pro Rylee Arnold, Ezra Frech and pro Daniella Karagach, Dewan and Chmerkovskiy and Shum and Johnson. The team received a perfect 40 out of 40.

While each couple delivered performances worthy of the Broadway stage, the show ultimately bid farewell to Stiles and Sosa.

“It’s been an incredible experience. I pulled things out of myself that I didn’t realize were there. Ezra is just an amazing person. I’m going to be sad not to see him every day,” Stiles said while becoming emotional.

Dancing With the Stars airs on ABC and Disney+ Tuesdays at 8 p.m. ET. Scroll down to see each couple’s scores from Disney Night:

#3608. How To Watch Sense And Sensibility (2026) At Home

There's a reason Jane Austen's 1811 novel "Sense and Sensibility" has been adapted so many times to the screen and the stage. The story of the Dashwood sisters, as they experience love and heartbreak after being forced to move away from their family estate and into the cottage of a relative, is as timeless in its coming of age story as it is timely and relatable in its themes and sharp social commentary.

There are many movies based on Jane Austen books, some retaining the period setting and others taking a more modern approach. The best Jane Austen movies are the ones that simply focus on the relatable and complex heroine and the hardships they endure. Case in point, Georgia Oakley's 2026 adaptation of "Sense and Sensibility" starring Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles as Elinor and Marianne. /Film's own Ben Pearson praised the film as one you absolutely should watch even in a crowded movie landscape, highlighting how "funny, charming, sweet, and full of suppressed yearning" this adaptation is, and even comparing it to Greta Gerwig's 2019 film adaptation of "Little Women."

After the film failed to make much of an impact in movie theaters, Focus Features is bringing "Sense and Sensibility" to digital platforms on November 3, 2026. Those wanting to actually own the movie rather than just lease it from a platform that can take it away from you at their whim, will have to wait until December 15, 2026 for Universal Pictures Home to release the film on Blu-ray.

It's been over 30 years since Ang Lee's phenomenal 1995 version of "Sense and Sensibility," but now we have a new take that offers a similarly gorgeous-looking movie adaptation. Georgia Oakley's movie  gives the relationship between the Dashwood sisters a bigger focus, especially in how they grow and learn from one another amid their respective romances.

The film also stars Caitríona Balfe, Frank Dillane, Herbert Nordrum, George MacKay, and Fiona Shaw — who has a standout scene. Even if "Sense and Sensibility" didn't really make a splash at the box office and doesn't make much of an impact during awards season, it is a tale worth experiencing, whether for the first time, or just for a new time.

The home video release of "Sense and Sensibility" also arrives with this bonus content at participating retailers.

#3607. This Ultra-Wide Samsung Gaming Monitor Is $600 Off

An ultra-wide curved gaming monitor with ridiculous specs is every gamer's dream, but they (usually) don't come cheap. The 57-inch Samsung Odyssey Neo G9, one of the best ultra-wide gaming monitors on the market, is currently on sale for $1,499.99 (originally $2,499.99 at launch)—that's its second-best discount, according to price-checking tools.

The Samsung Odyssey Neo G9 Series is not a regular ultra-wide gaming monitor. It has impressive specs, but you'll need a top-notch gaming computer with specific outputs to take full advantage of its 240Hz refresh rate potential.

This monitor came out in 2023 with an "excellent" review from PCMag, mainly due to its impressive 7,680 by 2,160 4K native resolution, the ridiculous 57-inch screen size, its great color range and accuracy, the 240Hz refresh rate, and its design. The VA panel also means you get a bright 1,000-nit screen. To make full use of its powerful 240Hz refresh rate, you'll need to use a DisplayPort 2.1, or you'll be limited to 120Hz. You'll also need a powerful modern graphics card that is able to push the frames at a native resolution to max out the monitor's potential.

Although it is pricey, this monitor is a great value for the right gamer. You'll need plenty of space to fit a 57-inch screen, as well as a powerful computer to justify using the monitor—if you're not a competitive gamer with a powerful computer, it's probably not worth the price tag. Instead, consider this Asus gaming monitor going for $329.99 (originally $499) right now.
